title: A workflow for residual stress control in laser powder bed fusion manufacturing
abstract: Abstract Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) enables near-net-shape manufacturing of complex metal components with exceptional geometric freedom. However, the rapid cyclic heating and cooling inherent to the process generates steep thermal gradients and plastic incompatibility, resulting in the accumulation of high residual stresses within printed components. These residual stresses can drive distortion and cracking, degrade fatigue performance, and reduce dimensional accuracy. Most existing studies attempt to mitigate residual stress using isolated approaches, which complicates their translation into robust manufacturing practice. This review therefore organizes residual stress mitigation into a system-level workflow spanning simulation, process optimization, material-level control, and post-treatment management. Multiscale simulation approaches can be employed to identify the dominant contributors to residual stress, thereby guiding the selection of in-process mitigation strategies and geometry design, including process parameter optimization, scan pattern and sequence design, and structural design. Material-level strategies, such as powder reuse governance, process atmosphere control, transformation engineering, and in situ alloying, are complementary approaches for stabilizing processing conditions and improving the consistency between simulation predictions and practical manufacturing environments. Post-treatment approaches, including stress-relief heat treatment, vibration-based methods, and surface peening techniques, can be further applied to achieve application-oriented residual stress control. These strategies should operate within a closed-loop framework in which experimental measurements are continuously fed back into the model to enable calibration and iterative refinement of process strategies. The integrated workflow proposed in this review provides a practical framework for residual-stress-controlled LPBF manufacturing, facilitating the transition from laboratory-scale optimization toward reliable and repeatable industrial production.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing enables the design and fabrication of high-value metal components with exceptional geometric freedom that is difficult or impossible to achieve through conventional subtractive manufacturing routes. Examples include conformal cooling channels, internal lattice architectures, graded-thickness structures, and part consolidation designs [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. Among various metal additive manufacturing processes, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) has become one of the most widely adopted techniques because it combines relatively high dimensional accuracy, fine feature resolution, and strong compatibility with a wide range of engineering alloys [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]. The localized laser melting and layer-by-layer consolidation enable near-net-shape fabrication with reduced tooling requirements and short iteration cycles, which is particularly advantageous for customized or low-volume production (Fig.  1 ) [ 9 ,  10 ]. As a result, LPBF has gradually evolved from a prototyping technology to a manufacturing method capable of producing functional end-use components. Representative applications include aerospace and space systems, orthopedic and dental implants, heat exchangers, turbine and combustor components, and energy-sector parts, where complex internal channels and lightweight structures are critical [ 11 ,  12 ]. However, despite the increasing maturity of machine platforms and process parameter databases, the reliability of LPBF-fabricated parts still depends strongly on controlling process-induced defects and internal stress states. In particular, residual stress remains a key barrier to broader qualification and industrial deployment of LPBF components [ 13 ,  14 – 15 ]. Residual stress in LPBF originates from the extreme thermal conditions generated by the moving laser heat source, repeated layer-wise reheating, and the mechanical constraints imposed by the previously solidified material and the build plate [ 16 ,  17 – 18 ]. Rapid localized heating followed by rapid cooling produces steep thermal gradients, and the resulting thermal strain cannot be accommodated uniformly throughout the material. When the transient thermal stress exceeds the temperature-dependent yield strength, plastic deformation occurs in and around the melt pool. The resulting irreversible strain is retained during cooling, generating residual stress due to deformation incompatibility [ 13 ,  14 ]. Beyond this classical temperature-gradient mechanism, residual stress is further intensified by several additional factors: (1) cyclic reheating and partial remelting, which repeatedly redistribute stress while progressively increasing structural constraint; (2) heterogeneous microstructure evolution and anisotropic elastic or plastic behavior arising from strong crystallographic texture and directional solidification; (3) phase transformations and associated volumetric changes, transformation-induced plasticity, or precipitation reactions; and (4) mismatches in thermal expansion and stiffness between the fabricated part and the substrate or support structures, which restrict thermal shrinkage. Residual stress can also be categorized according to spatial scale. Type I stresses occur at the macroscopic part scale and are responsible for global distortion. Type II stresses occur at the grain or microstructural scale and are associated with anisotropy and phase mismatch. Type III stresses arise at the sub-grain or defect scale and are related to dislocation structures and local heterogeneity produced by rapid solidification [ 19 ].

For LPBF-fabricated components, residual stress must be carefully managed to ensure geometric accuracy, structural integrity, and reliable service performance. During processing, residual stress can promote cracking, particularly in alloys with narrow ductility windows, strong solidification segregation, or transformation-induced brittleness. It may also cause recoater interference during the build process or even lead to building failure [ 15 ,  16 ]. After printing, high tensile residual stress can drive distortion and warpage, reducing the dimensional fidelity of the resultant components. Residual stress also interacts with surface conditions and internal defects, increasing the effective driving force for crack propagation. In susceptible environments, it may further contribute to stress corrosion cracking or hydrogen-assisted cracking [ 20 ,  21 – 22 ]. In practical applications, residual stress can cause part movement during support removal or machining, resulting in loss of dimensional tolerance, poor assembly fit, and increased scrap rates. It may also accelerate crack initiation and propagation under cyclic loading. These challenges highlight the need for comprehensive residual stress mitigation strategies that span simulation prediction, manufacturing strategy optimization, material-level optimization, and post-treatment management.

However, most existing studies focus on only one or two aspects in isolation, such as scan strategy optimization or stress-relief heat treatment. This fragmented approach limits transferability and may introduce conflicting trade-offs among residual stress, density, microstructure, and productivity. Therefore, it is necessary to establish a general workflow that connects predictive modeling with actionable design and processing decisions, and subsequently closes the loop through validation and post-processing. Such an approach would guide both future research and industrial practice toward residual stress-controlled LPBF manufacturing. Accordingly, this review provides an in-depth overview of representative strategies for mitigating residual stress in LPBF-fabricated components, including simulation-based prediction, process parameter optimization, raw material control, and post-treatment methods. The technical characteristics and comparative advantages of these approaches are systematically discussed, and a conceptual workflow for an integrated residual stress mitigation strategy is proposed. Finally, the current limitations of existing techniques and potential future directions for residual stress mitigation in LPBF are also highlighted.

sections.heading: Modeling for simulation prediction
paragraphs: To mitigate residual stress within LPBF-fabricated components, optimization of the printing process is required to reduce the effects of thermal gradients and deformation incompatibility between successive layers [ 15 ]. To evaluate the internal stress state, several post-process characterization techniques have been developed, including the hole-drilling method [ 23 ,  24 ], neutron diffraction [ 25 ], and X-ray diffraction (XRD) [ 26 ]. These methods can quantify the residual stress distribution and provide guidance for process parameter optimization. However, such post-process characterization techniques are often costly, and iterative trial-and-error optimization based on experimental measurements can be time-consuming [ 27 ]. Moreover, due to the highly complex melt pool dynamics and extremely rapid solidification during LPBF, direct experimental observation of the evolving stress state during processing is generally infeasible. Consequently, computational modeling has emerged as an indispensable tool for probing internal states that are experimentally inaccessible and for predicting residual stress evolution during the LPBF process [ 28 ].

Significant efforts have been devoted to accurately modeling the LPBF process due to its inherent complexity. This complexity arises from the multiphysics nature of the process, involving intricate interactions among thermal, mechanical, and fluid dynamic phenomena (Fig.  2 a) [ 27 ,  29 ]. Its multiscale characteristics require analysis across widely varying length scales. Meanwhile, many key physical phenomena occur on the order of microseconds, necessitating simulation frameworks capable of resolving extremely short temporal scales [ 30 ]. Consequently, addressing these physical complexities requires a systematic decomposition of the LPBF process into distinct and manageable simulation levels. In this section, three representative modeling approaches across macroscale, mesoscale, and microscale are introduced. Typically, macroscale models are employed to predict Type I stresses at the component scale, while mesoscale frameworks analyze the formation and evolution of Type I and Type II stresses. Microscale models are mainly used to investigate Type II and Type III stresses associated with microstructural heterogeneity and defect structures (Fig.  2 b) [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ]. These multiscale models are generally established based on the process-structure-property (PSP) relationship, which forms the fundamental framework of integrated computational materials engineering (ICME) [ 34 ]. By linking thermal history (process) with microstructural evolution (structure) and mechanical response (property), such simulations transform the qualitative PSP concept into a predictive tool for forecasting component performance, particularly in terms of minimizing residual stress. These multiscale modeling approaches therefore provide valuable insight into the mechanisms of stress evolution from different perspectives and offer important guidance for optimizing LPBF processes. sections.heading: Micro-scale simulation
paragraphs: Microscale simulation in LPBF aims to understand and quantify how thermal loading during rapid melting and solidification generates and evolves residual stress. Such simulations contribute to explaining the formation of both Type II and Type III stresses within the material microstructure. The heterogeneous mechanical response at the microscale is intrinsically linked to the complex microstructures generated by repeated rapid melting and solidification cycles. In particular, grain nucleation and subsequent evolution during solidification govern critical attributes such as local elastic anisotropy, crystallographic texture, and grain-boundary topology, all of which influence stress development and redistribution [ 35 ]. Collectively, these microstructural features act as dominant sources of stress concentration and strain incompatibility under subsequent thermal loading [ 36 ]. Consequently, the fidelity of thermal residual stress simulations depends strongly on how accurately the material microstructural state is captured. This observation motivates a more detailed investigation of microstructure evolution during solidification, which provides a necessary foundation for subsequent thermal stress analysis.

To capture microstructure evolution during LPBF, researchers have increasingly turned to advanced numerical frameworks capable of resolving the interface dynamics between liquid and solid phases. Among these approaches, the phase-field model (PFM) is widely recognized for its high-fidelity capability because it is grounded in multiphysics and thermodynamic principles. Early PFM studies in additive manufacturing established foundational relationships between basic process parameters and microstructural features [ 37 ,  38 ]. However, these early simulations were largely restricted to two-dimensional domains and relied on simplified thermal inputs extracted from separate macroscale models, which overlooked the complex thermal histories arising during layer-by-layer fabrication (Fig.  3 a,b). To address the limitations associated with simplified thermal inputs, Acharya et al. replaced the prescribed thermal field with temperature distributions obtained from preceding computational fluid dynamics (CFD) melt-pool simulations, which provided more realistic predictions of melt-pool geometry and temperature fields [ 39 ]. Similarly, Keller et al. used finite element method (FEM)-derived melt-pool thermal conditions to drive quantitative two-dimensional phase-field simulations of solidification [ 40 ]. Lu et al. further incorporated time-dependent temperature fields generated by laser scanning and preheating into a phase-field modeling framework (Fig.  3 c) [ 41 ]. By coupling melting, resolidification, and grain evolution under process-parameter-controlled thermal conditions, their model captured thermal accumulation effects during layer-by-layer fabrication. To further overcome the limitations of two-dimensional simulations, Liu et al. proposed a three-dimensional multiscale modeling framework that integrates finite-element-based thermal history predictions with microstructure simulations to explain site-specific grain textures, including vertical and inclined grain morphologies in complex geometries (Fig.  3 d) [ 42 ,  43 ]. Yang et al. further advanced this approach by coupling PFM with a high-fidelity thermal-fluid flow (TFF) model, enabling the simulation of the complete grain lifecycle, including nucleation and epitaxial growth (Fig.  3 e) [ 44 ]. More recently, Okugawa et al. coupled three-dimensional computational thermal–fluid dynamics (CTFD) melt-pool simulations with a two-dimensional multicomponent multiphase-field (MPF) model to quantitatively predict LPBF solidification microstructures [ 45 ]. This framework also extended microstructure prediction to layer-wise reheating effects by simulating remelting and resolidification during subsequent deposition cycles.

However, despite their high fidelity, phase-field simulations remain computationally expensive and often prohibitively time-consuming. To accelerate these simulations, machine learning (ML) techniques have recently been increasingly employed to approximate microstructure evolution and reduce computational costs [ 46 ,  47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ]. In addition, several alternative approaches have been applied under specific conditions, including Physically-Based Monte Carlo (PBMC) methods [ 51 ], kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) simulations [ 52 ], and two-dimensional cellular automata (CA) models [ 53 ]. Nevertheless, while microstructure simulations and experimental characterization can resolve spatial distributions, morphological features, and crystallographic textures with high fidelity, they primarily focus on microstructural kinetics and typically do not explicitly incorporate the coupled mechanical response. Therefore, establishing quantitative links between microstructural heterogeneity and thermal residual stress profiles requires the development of microstructure-informed mechanical frameworks that integrate microstructural evolution with stress analysis.

A prominent microscale mechanical modeling approach is the crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) [ 54 ,  55 ], which has become one of the most widely adopted micromechanical simulation tools for LPBF. Conventional CPFEM frameworks, however, are limited in capturing the transient mechanical response during additive manufacturing, as they typically assume static microstructures and fixed constitutive laws. In LPBF, the microstructure, dislocation density, and thermal field evolve continuously under the transient thermal cycles imposed during the printing process. Consequently, achieving physically predictive simulations requires CPFEM to be coupled with other modeling frameworks, such as PFM, dislocation density (DD) models, and CFD. Grilli et al. developed a dislocation-based crystal plasticity model at the grain scale to investigate cyclic loading behavior and low-cycle fatigue [ 56 ]. To validate CPFEM predictions, Chen et al. employed electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to map grain orientation and morphology at the microscale, which were subsequently used as inputs for CPFEM simulations to quantify intergranular and intragranular residual stresses in LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel [ 57 ]. Similarly, Grilli et al. integrated digital image correlation (DIC) with CPFEM to calibrate and validate slip–twin parameters [ 58 ].

Further developments have focused on incorporating process-dependent microstructural evolution. Grilli et al. developed a CPFEM framework incorporating element elimination and reactivation to simulate the melting and resolidification processes during LPBF (Fig.  4 ) [ 59 ]. In this model, temperature fields derived from thermal-fluid simulations [ 49 ] and grain structures obtained from PFM simulations [ 44 ] were used as inputs, and the predicted results were validated experimentally. Hu et al. subsequently employed a fully coupled multiphysics CPFEM framework to predict the evolution of Type II residual stress during LPBF, with results showing good agreement with experimental XRD measurements [ 60 ]. Building on this work, Hu et al. established a fully coupled multiscale and multiphysics modeling framework linking process parameters, microstructure evolution, and dislocation-based crystal plasticity [ 61 ]. More recently, Sun et al. further advanced this approach by developing a fully coupled multiphase-field CPFEM (MPF–CPFEM) framework featuring shared-mesh, real-time data exchange and an element-free Galerkin-finite difference method (EFG–FDM) treatment of nonlocal derivatives [ 62 ]. This framework enables concurrent prediction of evolving microstructures and thermomechanical responses during multi-track LPBF processing. It should be noted that although CPFEM is fundamentally a phenomenological approach, it remains highly effective for simulating thermomechanical responses when temperature-dependent material properties and thermal expansion-induced strains are properly incorporated. Accordingly, several CPFEM variants have been developed to capture microstructural strengthening mechanisms, including geometrically necessary dislocation (GND)-based CPFEM models [ 63 ,  64 ] and statistically stored dislocation (SSD)-based CPFEM models [ 65 ]. These frameworks can also be applied to investigate thermal stress evolution and residual stress formation during LPBF processing. Overall, microscale simulations of residual stress are increasingly evolving toward predictive, computationally efficient, and experimentally validated digital twin frameworks that integrate process physics, microstructure evolution, and microstructure-sensitive constitutive behavior within a unified modeling environment. As these capabilities continue to mature, microscale models are expected to provide not only mechanistic insights into the origin and evolution of Type II and Type III residual stresses, but also robust and quantitatively transferable inputs for downstream property and performance assessments, including fatigue behavior, cracking susceptibility, and distortion prediction, as well as for closed-loop process optimization.

sections.heading: Meso-scale simulation
paragraphs: Mesoscale (track-scale) simulation provides a critical link between microscale physics-based models and macroscale engineering performance predictions by explicitly resolving process phenomena that are typically homogenized at the part scale [ 66 ]. In LPBF, this regime generally spans length scales from approximately 10 μm to 1 mm, corresponding to individual scan tracks. Within this range, melt-pool heat transfer and thermofluid flow can be directly modeled to obtain the transient melt-pool geometry and thermal gradients that govern solidification behavior [ 67 ]. Solidification parameters, such as thermal gradients, interface velocities, and cooling rates, can be extracted from the predictions of transient melt-pool geometry and thermal histories. These parameters are then used to drive microscale microstructure models that predict grain morphology and crystallographic texture evolution. In parallel, mesoscale simulation outputs can be condensed into reduced-order representations, including calibrated heat source parameters and layer-wise inherent strain distributions. These quantities can subsequently be incorporated into macroscale thermomechanical models to predict part-scale temperature histories and residual stress under realistic scan strategies, while avoiding the computational expense of explicitly resolving melt-pool fluid flow throughout the entire build process.

Thermomechanical simulations based on the FEM can simplify thermal modeling by employing an explicit moving heat source representation. This approach enables the simulation of scan-path-dependent thermal cycling that drives residual stress accumulation. However, it is limited by the need for predefined geometries and its strong sensitivity to heat source definitions and boundary conditions [ 68 ,  69 ]. To account for complex geometrical evolution induced by melting, remelting, solidification, and melt-pool convection, the quiet element method (QEM), also known as the element elimination and reactivation method, has been incorporated within the FEM framework [ 70 ]. This technique allows inactive or non-contributing elements to be dynamically activated as the build progresses, enabling the mechanical model to represent incremental geometric changes without requiring remeshing. To further mitigate input uncertainty, Denlinger et al. employed experimentally calibrated boundary conditions in thermal models to capture evolving thermal histories more accurately [ 70 ]. Hocine et al. used operando XRD to evaluate competing volumetric heat source parameterizations and refine the resulting thermal histories used for residual stress prediction [ 71 ]. However, this approach primarily focuses on validating thermal and phase evolution rather than performing full three-dimensional residual stress mapping. Alternative numerical approaches have also been explored. For example, Li et al. predicted three-dimensional thermal, mechanical, and displacement fields of SLM-printed titanium alloys using the differential quadrature method (DQM) (Fig.  5 a) [ 72 ]. Building upon this approach, Li et al. first determined temperature-dependent effective material properties of functionally graded nickel/titanium alloys (FGNTAs) using the rule of mixtures, and then employed DQM to predict the temperature distribution, residual stress, and deformation fields within the as-built FGNTAs [ 29 ]. To further integrate melt-pool heat transfer and fluid flow with mechanical response, coupled thermo-fluid-mechanical frameworks have emerged as a prominent approach for improving the accuracy of residual stress prediction. The temperature fields obtained from thermo-fluid simulations are mapped onto the mechanical FEM model and serve as thermal loads, providing spatially and temporally resolved material properties within the mechanical analysis. This coupling enables accurate representation of thermal histories while incorporating realistic geometric features, including surface roughness, internal porosity, and voids. Because the repetitive thermal cycling inherent to LPBF drives the progressive accumulation of thermal and residual stresses, accurately capturing the temperature field history is a critical prerequisite for reliable mechanical simulations [ 73 ]. To improve the fidelity of thermal analysis, multiphysics thermo-fluid simulations based on CFD are frequently employed to predict the transient temperature fields associated with melt-pool dynamics.

Early investigations primarily focused on understanding melt-flow-driven defect mechanisms, such as spatter formation, powder denudation, and porosity generation. For example, Khairallah et al. developed a three-dimensional powder-scale model that couples the moving laser heat source with melt flow, Marangoni convection, and recoil pressure effects to predict transient temperature fields and melt-pool dynamics [ 74 ]. However, in many early models, the laser absorptivity was assumed to be constant, despite the fact that multiple reflections as well as vapor and plasma plume effects can significantly alter the effective energy absorption, thereby influencing the resulting thermal gradients. To address this limitation, Liu et al. introduced an in-solver multi-reflection ray-tracing heat source model capable of computing spatially and temporally resolved absorbed energy in real time [ 75 ]. Building on advances in powder spreading simulations based on the discrete element method (DEM), thermo-fluid models have subsequently been coupled with DEM frameworks to construct powder-scale models capable of simulating the full LPBF process [ 76 ]. Yu et al. further proposed a volume-of-fluid computational fluid dynamics (VOF-CFD) model combined with ray tracing and Fresnel reflection to more physically describe laser absorption and melt-pool evolution (Fig.  5 b) [ 77 ].

To reduce the computational cost of such high-fidelity simulations, Gallego et al. employed adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) together with an equivalent absorptivity surrogate model that efficiently captures multi-reflection absorption behavior [ 78 ]. Although this approach significantly reduces runtime, it introduces calibration dependence and may omit certain melt-pool instability phenomena. In addition, to incorporate the effects of vaporization and plume flow [ 79 ], Bidare et al. developed a multiphysics thermo-fluid model that couples the laser plume and inert-gas atmosphere by solving the compressible Navier-Stokes equations with species transport and an energy equation for heat transfer in the gas domain [ 80 ]. Building upon these thermo-fluid modeling approaches, Chen et al. first employed a three-dimensional spatial interpolation method to extract transient temperature fields from melt-pool simulations and map them into a mechanical FEM framework to predict track-scale residual stress (Fig.  5 c) [ 27 ]. To simplify the thermal–mechanical coupling process, Yang et al. developed a finite volume (FV)-based framework that integrates thermal-fluid simulations with subsequent mechanical analysis [ 81 ]. Kishore et al. further investigated residual stress accumulation and its evolution in LPBF-fabricated multilayer thin-wall structures using a conforming mesh modeling strategy (Fig.  5 d) [ 82 ]. In their framework, powder-bed generation based on the DEM is combined with a VOF-CFD melt-pool model. The resulting thermo-fluid simulation outputs are then coupled with FEM analysis to predict residual stress development during the LPBF process.

In summary, mesoscale LPBF modeling provides a critical bridge between microstructure physics and part-scale performance by resolving track-level thermal-fluid phenomena and translating the resulting thermal histories into predictions of microstructure evolution and residual stress development. Thermo-fluid-mechanical frameworks remain the dominant approach for residual stress assessment because they convert transient temperature fields into thermal loads and temperature-dependent material properties within mechanical simulations. First, the accuracy of predicted thermal histories is expected to improve as laser-matter interaction models incorporate more realistic physics, including multi-reflection effects, evolving absorptivity, keyhole dynamics, vapor and plume shielding, and powder-to-solid phase transitions through parameterizations that are internally consistent and transferable across different machines and material systems. Second, residual stress prediction is expected to evolve beyond purely elastic or simplified plasticity models toward more robust temperature-dependent constitutive formulations, such as creep-enabled models that capture cyclic thermal loading, high-temperature stress relaxation, and strain accumulation during repeated reheating events. The development of standardized high-temperature constitutive datasets for additively manufactured alloys will be essential to support these advances. Third, geometry handling will likely progress from heuristic element activation schemes toward topology-consistent evolving-domain approaches capable of representing realistic track morphology, keyhole-induced porosity, and surface roughness without introducing excessive numerical diffusion.

sections.heading: Macro-scale simulation
paragraphs: Macro-scale simulation focuses on predicting part-scale residual stresses that lead to global distortion in LPBF-fabricated components. In principle, the mesoscale modeling methods described in the previous section can be extended to predict macro-scale residual stresses. However, the computational cost of resolving track-scale thermo-fluid phenomena throughout an entire build is typically prohibitive, often requiring simulation times ranging from several weeks to months [ 83 ]. To address this limitation, Patil et al. presented benchmark coupled simulations of multi-track and multi-layer builds and evaluated several widely used modeling approximations, thereby providing a practical foundation for subsequent method development [ 84 ]. To further reduce computational cost, the inherent strain method (ISM) has been widely adopted. Originally developed for predicting residual deformation and stress in metal welding processes [ 85 ,  86 ], ISM enables rapid prediction of residual stress and distortion through a single elastic simulation.

Inherent strain refers to the permanent plastic strain retained in a material element after cooling from the rapid thermal cycles experienced during LPBF. For any element, the total strain   ε t  induced by instantaneous thermal expansion can theoretically be decomposed into several components: elastic strain ε e , plastic strain   ε p , thermal strain   ε T , phase transformation strain  ε pt  and creep strain   ε c  [ 87 ]. In the final cooled state, the elastic strain   ε e  and thermal strain   ε T  are generally considered recoverable because they contribute minimally to permanent deformation. In many LPBF simulations, the phase transformation strain   ε pt  is neglected, while creep strain   ε c  is treated as a time-dependent component. Consequently, the inherent strain   ε * is commonly defined as the irreversible plastic strain  ε p  generated by material yielding under rapid heating and cooling cycles. However, several studies, often referred to as the modified inherent strain method (MISM), suggest that elastic strain is not completely relieved when the component cools to ambient temperature [ 87 ,  88 ]. In this framework, the inherent strain is expressed as   ε * =  ε p  +  ε (i,e) − ε (s,e) , where i and s denote the intermediate and steady-state periods, respectively. The validity of the MISM has been further demonstrated through numerical simulations and experimental validation (Fig.  6 a–c). At present, one of the most challenging issues in the ISM is the accurate determination and appropriate application of the inherent strain values. In practice, inherent strain is influenced by multiple factors, including scanning strategy [ 89 ], process parameters [ 90 ], material properties [ 91 ], part geometry [ 92 ], and even geometric features such as overhang angles [ 93 ,  94 – 95 ]. Consequently, the inherent strain value can be determined through experimental measurements [ 96 ], high-fidelity thermo-mechanical simulations [ 87 ], or empirical approaches based on process observations [ 97 ]. To ensure the predictive accuracy of the method, a calibration procedure is typically required before applying the inherent strain values to large-scale components. The conventional ISM framework generally involves two primary steps [ 98 ]. First, the inherent strain tensor is experimentally determined by measuring the residual stress or distortion of a representative small-scale specimen fabricated under identical process conditions. Second, the extracted plastic strain tensor is applied to a part-scale finite element model within a linear elastic analysis to predict the distortion and residual stress distribution in components with complex geometries. Building upon this framework, Panagiotis et al. proposed an element-birth technique based on the inherent strain concept to simulate the layer-by-layer material deposition process [ 99 ]. This approach sequentially activates elements during the build simulation while imposing the inherent strain field, enabling the prediction of residual stress and distortion evolution throughout the printing process. Notably, the numerical predictions show strong agreement with experimental measurements, while the computational cost is significantly lower than that of detailed thermo-mechanical simulations.

The ISM is further implemented in FEM software to enable efficient prediction of residual stress and distortion in additive manufacturing. Its implementation generally involves three main steps. First, the inherent strain components are determined from experimental measurements or high-fidelity thermo-mechanical simulations and are then prescribed in the structural model as initial strain fields or equivalent thermal loads. Second, the sequential material deposition process is simulated using an element-birth technique, in which inherent strains are incrementally imposed as each new layer is activated. Finally, a static linear elastic analysis is conducted to approximate the residual stress distribution after cooling. In practical applications, different commercial FEM platforms provide distinct workflows for implementing the ISM. For example, ABAQUS commonly employs user-defined subroutines such as UEXPAN or UMAT, or applies predefined initial strain conditions. ANSYS typically introduces the strain field through a thermal expansion analogy or by using APDL-based scripting procedures. MSC Marc/Mentat represents inherent strain as equivalent loads or temperature fields combined with simplified element activation schemes. Meanwhile, Simufact Additive provides a dedicated additive manufacturing module that streamlines the estimation and application of inherent strains within an integrated simulation workflow.

Although commercial finite element analysis (FEA) packages have incorporated the ISM for industrial-scale component simulations, the proprietary nature of their implementations often obscures the detailed methodologies used for extracting and applying inherent strains in part-scale modeling. Consequently, subsequent research efforts have focused on refining and validating this approach. For example, Siewert et al. advanced the mechanical layer-equivalent model by incorporating experimentally calibrated inherent strains obtained from LPBF-fabricated cantilever beams [ 100 ]. Their numerical simulations demonstrated high accuracy in predicting residual deformation when compared with experimental measurements. Similarly, Ahmad et al. reported strong agreement between residual stress distributions predicted by the ISM and those measured using the contour method, revealing tensile residual stresses near surface edges and compressive stresses in the central regions of the specimens (Fig.  6 d,e) [ 101 ]. More recently, a growing research trend has emerged toward integrating high-fidelity, experimentally validated finite element models with ML algorithms. Such hybrid frameworks offer the potential to develop computationally efficient reduced-order models capable of rapidly predicting residual stress and distortion, thereby enabling practical deployment within design optimization and process control frameworks.

sections.heading: Building precess optimization
paragraphs: Multiscale simulation provides a powerful numerical tool for predicting thermal residual stress and elucidating process-structure-property relationships in LPBF. Consequently, simulation-based optimization has become an essential approach for achieving predictable and targeted residual stress mitigation, offering a more accurate and controlled strategy compared with traditional procedural adjustments, such as substrate preheating [ 102 ,  103 – 104 ], remelting [ 105 ,  106 ], and parallel scanning strategies [ 107 ,  108 ]. The primary objective of computational modeling is to clarify the physical mechanisms governing residual stress formation and to accurately predict the resulting stress distribution within printed components. Once validated against experimental measurements, these predictive models can be leveraged to systematically guide optimization strategies. In particular, they enable the rational refinement of manufacturing conditions, including process parameters, scanning strategies, and structural design, thereby facilitating more effective control of residual stress during LPBF fabrication.

sections.heading: Process parameters optimization
paragraphs: Optimization of LPBF process parameters represents one of the most direct approaches for improving manufacturing quality and mitigating residual stress. However, due to the intrinsic complexity of the layer-by-layer fabrication process, in which beam-driven heat transfer, phase transformations, and temperature-dependent plasticity are strongly coupled, it is essential to quantify the individual contribution of each parameter to the overall thermomechanical response. For example, Vastola et al. systematically quantified the characteristics of thermal stress fields influenced by beam size, laser power density, scanning speed, and chamber bed temperature in Ti-6Al-4V components [ 109 ]. Oliveira et al. further reviewed the influence of general processing parameters on the formation of residual stress and provided guidance for parameter optimization strategies (Fig.  7 a,b) [ 110 ]. In particular, the nonlinear interactions between laser power and scanning speed play a dominant role in determining melt pool geometry and the magnitude of thermal gradients during fabrication. Consequently, process-induced defects such as incomplete fusion, spheroidization, crack-like voids, and keyhole porosity often exhibit complex correlations with the evolution of residual stress in LPBF components [ 111 ]. FEM can be employed to numerically solve mathematical models describing the LPBF process and to support parameter optimization. However, macro-scale FEM simulations often deviate from experimental observations because they rely on modeling assumptions and simplifications that are necessary to maintain computational tractability [ 112 ]. Although high-fidelity approaches such as CFD have become increasingly sophisticated, their application is typically limited to simulations of single tracks or a small number of layers due to the substantial computational cost involved [ 113 ]. Consequently, ML models have increasingly been introduced to optimize manufacturing parameters, particularly for controlling critical material characteristics such as residual stress fields [ 114 ], surface defects [ 115 ], and microstructure evolution (Fig.  7 c,d) [ 49 ]. Early investigations in this area were largely empirical in nature [ 116 ], relying heavily on extensive experimental datasets and statistical approaches such as design of experiments (DoE). For instance, some studies have developed LPBF optimization systems for Ti-6Al-4V based on supervised deep neural networks (SDNN) [ 117 ]. These systems are typically trained on experimentally derived datasets to predict material properties, such as relative density, from multiple process parameters. However, the current studies on ML-assisted process optimization have largely focused on directed energy deposition (DED) processes and have more frequently targeted defect mitigation and tensile strength optimization. In comparison, relatively limited research has addressed the integration of thermal residual stress analysis in LPBF with ML-based optimization frameworks, highlighting a clear research gap in this area.

Looking ahead, a practical and scalable route for residual stress mitigation is likely to rely on hybrid, physics-informed reduced-order modeling frameworks. These approaches retain the essential governing physical relationships while replacing repeatedly executed, computationally intensive thermo-mechanical simulations with rapidly evaluable surrogate predictors that can be embedded within iterative optimization loops, such as those involving scan path planning or multi-track thermal field predictions. In parallel, improved calibration of heat-source representations will be critical for enhancing model reliability. In particular, Bayesian optimization and probabilistic updating methods offer promising strategies for systematically refining model parameters, thereby reducing the persistent discrepancies between simulation and experimental observations that currently limit the credibility and transferability of parameter optimization results. As surrogate modeling techniques continue to advance, part-scale prediction of residual stress fields across complex geometries is expected to become feasible. For example, convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures capable of learning spatially distributed fields may enable stress-aware optimization at design-relevant scales, rather than restricting predictions to single-track or few-layer scenarios. Finally, the emergence of closed-loop decision-making strategies, including reinforcement learning frameworks that autonomously select process parameters to achieve desired melt-pool or thermal field targets, indicates a shift from one-time offline optimization toward adaptive, measurement-informed process control in LPBF manufacturing [ 118 ].

sections.heading: Topology optimization
paragraphs: In addition to process parameters, the macroscopic distribution of residual stress is strongly influenced by structural topology. In geometrically complex components, the transient thermal history becomes strongly coupled with the spatial layout, support configuration, and build orientation, which collectively govern local heat accumulation and the evolution of structural stiffness during fabrication [ 119 ]. Therefore, geometric design must simultaneously consider both functional performance and manufacturability. Within this context, integrating manufacturing constraints into the design process, commonly referred to as design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), is essential for ensuring dimensional accuracy and structural integrity in the as-built state. Topology optimization (TO) has emerged as an efficient numerical approach for identifying optimal material distributions under specific manufacturing constraints [ 120 ,  121 ]. To mitigate local cracking and warping caused by thermal stresses, optimization strategies that couple TO with thermo-mechanical stress analysis have been proposed, aiming to homogenize the stress field throughout the structure. For example, Allaire et al. formulated a level-set topology optimization framework that integrates coupled thermo-mechanical models, enabling significant mitigation of thermal residual stresses and vertical deformation [ 122 ]. Similarly, Khalilvandi et al. proposed a sequential TO framework that combines Peridynamics (PD) with thermo-mechanical analysis to minimize thermally induced stresses during additive manufacturing (Fig.  8 a,b) [ 123 ]. Although these studies employ high-fidelity models to predict thermal stresses, such approaches often involve substantial computational cost. To improve computational efficiency, several studies have attempted to replace detailed thermo-mechanical simulations with the ISM. For example, Misiun et al. applied ISM to predict thermal distortion and incorporated distortion constraints within a Solid Isotropic Material with Penalization (SIMP) topology optimization framework [ 124 ]. This approach was subsequently extended to thermal stress management [ 125 ] and further integrated into level-set topology optimization frameworks [ 126 ]. Despite its computational efficiency and widespread adoption, ISM suffers from a key limitation in that the inherent strain values are highly sensitive to process parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, and scanning strategy. Consequently, any change in processing conditions typically requires recalibration of the inherent strain parameters, which reduces the generalizability of the approach. To overcome this calibration dependency, more recent studies have shifted toward design strategies that enhance heat dissipation during the additive manufacturing process. For instance, Ranjan et al. proposed a physics-based three-dimensional topology optimization framework that integrates a simplified steady-state thermal model to detect and mitigate local overheating [ 127 ,  128 ]. Similarly, Das et al. developed a physics-motivated geometric method that estimates local thermal conductivity based on geometric features, thereby enabling the identification and mitigation of overheating risks during fabrication [ 119 ].

However, numerous studies have reported that enforcing thermal stress constraints during optimization often adversely affects mechanical performance, particularly structural stiffness. To address this tradeoff, an alternative strategy involves introducing sacrificial materials or support structures that function as mechanical anchors to restrain thermally induced deformation in the primary structure. For example, Cheng et al. combined the ISM with the Finite Cell Method (FCM) to predict thermal stress fields, enabling the simultaneous optimization of support topology and build orientation (Fig.  8 c–e) [ 129 ]. Similarly, Zhou et al. integrated transient heat conduction simulation (HCS) with a novel overhang constraint to design support structures capable of reducing thermal gradients and enhancing heat dissipation during fabrication [ 130 ]. Subedi et al. proposed an alternative strategy by transforming transient thermal histories into equivalent static loads, allowing the design of material-efficient support structures while maintaining adequate thermal performance and build stability [ 131 ]. In addition, Wang et al. applied a heat-source-based formulation at the interface between host and support structures to constrain the maximum temperature within the support region, thereby facilitating more effective thermal dissipation [ 132 ].

The optimization strategy can be further advanced by jointly considering scanning strategies and structural topology. For example, Chen et al. optimized both free-form scanning paths and structural topology using a level-set method [ 133 ]. However, the resulting scanning paths often fail to accommodate practical material infill patterns and may lead to surface defects. Although simplified thermal models, such as the ISM and heat conduction simulations, significantly improve computational efficiency, traditional topology optimization frameworks still face prohibitive computational costs due to the repeated FEA required in iterative optimization loops [ 134 ]. To address this challenge, Yao et al. proposed a hybrid ML approach for additive manufacturing design feature recommendation during the conceptual design stage, combining hierarchical clustering with support vector machines (SVM) [ 135 ]. More broadly, generative design methods have been increasingly explored to develop high-performance structures tailored for additive manufacturing [ 136 ,  137 ,  138 ,  139 – 140 ].

AI-driven design frameworks can alleviate computational burdens by functioning as surrogate models or by employing advanced architectures such as Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). For instance, Dong et al. developed a feature-based surrogate model using a three-dimensional U-Net CNN to accurately predict thermal residual stress distributions in LPBF components. The model was trained on representative geometric primitives, such as struts and wall structures, enabling efficient prediction across more complex geometries [ 141 ]. These developments suggest that future design frameworks should emphasize the co-optimization of topology, support structures, and scanning strategies. In such integrated approaches, sacrificial anchors, heat dissipation pathways, and scan sequencing can be treated as complementary design variables rather than independent downstream decisions. Collectively, these advances point toward practical digital design workflows capable of delivering manufacturable, high-performance structures with controlled residual stress at the part scale.

sections.heading: Scan strategy optimization
paragraphs: Although DfAM significantly improves manufacturability and build quality, the associated design modifications may negatively affect structural mechanical properties, particularly structural stiffness. To mitigate these trade-offs, scanning path optimization is often employed to refine the process and reduce thermally induced residual stresses. One critical advancement in process control is the optimization of the inter-layer scan rotation angle, which has a strong influence on residual stress evolution. By rotating the scan direction between successive layers, thermally induced shrinkage strains can be redistributed across multiple orientations, promoting a more uniform stress field and reducing directional stress accumulation. Parry et al. [ 68 ] used thermo-mechanical simulations to show that while alternating scan directions primarily influence the spatial distribution rather than the absolute magnitude of residual stress, minimizing the scanning vector length remains the most effective strategy for reducing the dominant longitudinal stress component.

Similarly, Ali et al. [ 142 ] demonstrated that employing a 90° alternating scanning strategy combined with short scan vectors significantly reduces thermal residual stress accumulation in Ti-6Al-4V components. Robinson et al. [ 143 ] further introduced a “suitability measure” for evaluating scan angles and reported that certain rotation angles, such as 67°, may provide improved stress redistribution compared with conventional alternating strategies. However, scan rotation angles remain crucial primarily for mitigating directional stress anisotropy. In a subsequent study, Robinson et al. [ 97 ] confirmed that the XY alternating strategy produces the lowest and most uniform residual stress distribution among the multi-directional strategies examined, suggesting that a simple 90° rotation may be sufficient to suppress stress anisotropy. It should be noted that the optimal rotation angle may vary depending on the material system. For example, Serrano et al. reported that a 67° rotation generated lower peak residual stresses than a 90° rotation in Inconel 718 components, indicating that scan strategy optimization should be tailored to specific materials and processing conditions [ 144 ].

Another widely investigated approach is the chessboard (or island) scanning strategy. In this method, the exposure area is divided into discrete subregions, commonly referred to as islands, which are subsequently scanned using a zigzag raster pattern. In principle, this segmentation reduces large-scale thermal gradients by promoting more uniform heat distribution and enabling localized heat dissipation. For instance, Ramos et al. introduced an intermittent scanning strategy that reduces heat accumulation by algorithmically selecting non-adjacent scan islands based on distance-weighted criteria [ 145 ]. This approach achieved a 42% reduction in deformation compared with conventional unidirectional scanning and a 10% improvement over alternating scanning strategies when using a 0.1 mm scan vector. However, Robinson et al. reported that conventional chessboard strategies may generate thermal stresses comparable to, or even higher than, those produced by a simple 90° alternating scanning strategy (Fig.  9 a,b) [ 97 ]. In contrast, Liu et al. demonstrated that an optimized “interval island” strategy reduced residual deformation by up to 7.7% compared with conventional stripe scanning methods [ 146 ]. These findings indicate that the effectiveness of island-based scanning strategies strongly depends on the specific scanning sequence and thermal management within each island, making scan ordering and island interaction critical factors governing thermal stress evolution. Recent advances in AI have significantly influenced the development of scanning strategies in LPBF. One notable achievement in intelligent scan path optimization is the SmartScan framework. Raman et al. combined physics-based and data-driven thermal models to perform intelligent optimization of scanning sequences (Fig.  9 c,d) [ 147 ]. This methodology was subsequently extended to multi-laser systems [ 148 ] and further adapted for part-scale applications [ 149 ]. With the increasing flexibility of scanning strategies, adaptive scan path generation methods have also been proposed to minimize thermal gradients during fabrication. For example, Qin et al. developed an adaptive toolpath generation algorithm that minimizes thermal gradients through numerical optimization combined with island-based sequencing [ 150 ]. Experimental results demonstrated a 46% reduction in distortion compared with conventional zigzag scanning patterns, while maintaining comparable mechanical properties. More recently, deep learning-based approaches have been introduced to enable autonomous process optimization. Ogoke et al. proposed a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework capable of deriving control policies for dynamically adjusting laser velocity and power, thereby stabilizing melt-pool depth and mitigating overheating-induced defects [ 151 ]. Similarly, Qin et al. developed a DRL-based strategy for generating thermally uniform scan patterns in LPBF [ 152 ]. Experimental validation showed that the optimized strategy reduced part distortion by approximately 47%, 29%, and 17% compared with conventional zigzag, chessboard, and adaptive toolpath generation strategies, respectively.

Looking ahead, scan strategy optimization is likely to evolve from static, rule-based prescriptions, such as fixed rotation angles or predefined chessboard layouts, toward adaptive, model-based decision-making frameworks that are both geometry-aware and uncertainty-aware. First, there is a clear trend toward intelligent scan sequencing frameworks that integrate reduced-order thermo-mechanical models with optimization techniques and model order reduction. Such approaches enable part-scale scan sequence planning within practical computational time budgets and can be extended to complex scenarios, including multi-layer builds and multi-laser systems. Second, learning-based methods are expected to progress beyond proof-of-concept demonstrations toward constrained policy optimization. In these frameworks, reinforcement learning algorithms are trained using process-consistent thermal surrogate models while incorporating manufacturing constraints, such as contour–infill logic, jump rules, and recoater safety considerations. This ensures that the optimized toolpaths remain practically manufacturable while simultaneously improving thermal uniformity and reducing residual stress. Third, future research is likely to frame scan strategy design as a multi-objective control problem that simultaneously balances residual stress and distortion against other critical metrics, including density, microstructure quality, and manufacturing productivity. Achieving this goal will require comprehensive experimental datasets that capture thermal signals, distortion behavior, and residual stress evolution under systematically varied scanning strategies. Collectively, these developments indicate that residual stress mitigation through scan strategy optimization will become increasingly predictive, scalable, and transferable across different alloys and geometries by integrating physics-based reduced models, data-driven policy learning, and part-scale experimental validation.

sections.heading: Real-time control
paragraphs: Since pre-process optimization is predominantly grounded in deterministic numerical simulations, it often underrepresents stochastic sources of process variability, such as powder-bed heterogeneity, spatter generation, and fluctuations in boundary conditions. Consequently, real-time feedback control (RTC) based on in-situ monitoring has become necessary to compensate for these uncertainties and bridge the gap between simulation predictions and actual manufacturing outcomes (Fig.  10 ) [ 153 ]. The application of RTC in additive manufacturing can be traced back to early developments in DED. Bi et al. evaluated infrared sensing techniques and implemented photodiode-based temperature regulation to prevent undesired substrate melting during deposition [ 154 ]. Subsequently, Fathi et al. advanced camera-based height control by employing a feedforward proportional-integral-derivative (PID) strategy, followed by the implementation of a sliding-mode controller to regulate clad geometry more robustly [ 155 ]. Hofman et al. further demonstrated a vision-based control system capable of maintaining melt-pool width at a prescribed reference value, compensating for local heat-sink variations on sub-second time scales (approximately 0.1 s) and enabling uniform dilution control along extended tracks [ 156 ]. Collectively, these studies demonstrated the practical feasibility of closed-loop control in cladding processes and established the methodological foundation for the development of RTC strategies in metal additive manufacturing. However, the extremely high scanning velocities characteristic of LPBF (typically 600–10,000 mm/s) impose stringent latency constraints on sensing, data processing, and control actuation. These limitations make the experimental implementation of complex closed-loop control algorithms particularly challenging. Consequently, the validation of many adaptive control strategies remains largely restricted to computational simulations. Future research should expand sensing modalities beyond the currently adopted configurations by integrating complementary monitoring signals, such as photodiode-based emissivity measurements and acoustic emission sensing. The development of cost-effective and compact hardware architectures will also be essential to improve scalability and enable broader industrial deployment. In parallel, continued advances in ML and digital twin technologies are expected to facilitate predictive model-based control strategies capable of leveraging synchronized multi-channel monitoring data. Collectively, these developments suggest that real-time control in LPBF will gradually evolve from laboratory-scale demonstrations toward robust, industrially viable implementations capable of compensating for process variability and ensuring consistent part quality.

sections.heading: Material-level optimization
paragraphs: Although simulations can effectively predict residual stress formation in LPBF, they are typically conducted under idealized process conditions and assume uniform raw material states. However, the actual manufacturing environment is considerably more complex and subject to various sources of uncertainty. Therefore, careful control of raw materials and processing conditions is essential to ensure consistency with simulation predictions while minimizing additional residual stresses arising from steep thermal gradients, repeated thermal cycling, and constrained shrinkage. Stabilizing melt-pool behavior, reducing stochastic variations in energy absorption, and tailoring thermo-physical material properties can help regulate the process conditions and thereby alleviate or compensate for thermally induced stresses. Furthermore, appropriate alloy design can introduce transformation-induced strain relaxation mechanisms that contribute to stress mitigation during cooling. Accordingly, material-level strategies for residual stress control primarily include powder reuse and feedstock integrity management, atmosphere control during processing, transformation engineering through alloy design, the use of inoculants and grain refiners, as well as in-situ alloying and compositional tailoring.

sections.heading: Feedstock quality management
paragraphs: Powder condition is a critical factor influencing the variability of residual stress in LPBF, as it directly affects absorptivity, packing density, layer uniformity, melt-pool stability, and the likelihood of local lack-of-fusion defects. These factors alter thermal gradients and constraint conditions in a spatially heterogeneous manner, which ultimately translates into heterogeneous residual stress distributions within the printed component. Therefore, maintaining consistent feedstock quality, particularly when using reused powders, is essential. During repeated reuse cycles, powders typically accumulate spatter and condensate particles, experience broadening of particle size distribution (PSD) due to agglomeration or partial sintering, undergo changes in surface chemistry, and may exhibit compositional drift in reactive alloys. These changes can significantly influence the optical absorption and thermal conductivity of the powder bed, while also increasing the probability of defects such as porosity and lack-of-fusion. Such defects can locally intensify tensile residual stresses and promote distortion in the fabricated parts [ 157 ,  158 ]. Consequently, effective powder reuse management should adopt a process-oriented strategy that considers not only powder properties but also their interactions with processing conditions, thereby ensuring consistent feedstock behavior and improving the overall quality and reliability of LPBF-manufactured components.

Overflow and spatter powders are typically chemically and morphologically distinct from the general reused powder population, and their improper reuse can introduce additional stresses into the resulting components. Gruber et al. investigated the characteristics of IN718 virgin, used, overflow, and spatter powders, demonstrating that spatter and overflow powders exhibit markedly different oxidation behaviors. These variations in surface chemistry have direct implications for process repeatability and thermal history control during LPBF (Fig.  11 a) [ 159 ]. For stainless steels such as 316L, Douglas et al. examined the evolution of powder properties during reuse cycles and reported that component performance remains relatively stable when reuse is properly managed. However, variability increases if spatter particles are not effectively removed, and uncontrolled atmospheric conditions may induce chemical changes that ultimately degrade material properties [ 160 ]. In aluminum alloys, oxide layer growth can exert an even stronger influence on laser absorption and melt-pool wetting behavior, amplifying variability in melt-pool dynamics and the resulting stress state. Consequently, stricter powder reuse governance is typically required for these materials. In practical applications, feedstock quality management requires integrated control of PSD, particle circularity thresholds, and the fraction of spatter or overflow powders within the reused feedstock. Several mitigation strategies have been reported in the literature, including (1) sieving and classification to remove large spatter particles and agglomerates; (2) controlled refresh ratios, in which a defined fraction of virgin powder is blended with reused powder; (3) segregation of powders by alloy system and reuse cycle to prevent cross-contamination; and (4) implementation of powder traceability systems incorporating reuse-cycle counts and oxygen-content monitoring. From the perspective of residual stress control, the key operational principle is to minimize stochastic thermal “hot spots” and “cold spots” caused by inhomogeneous powder layers. Powder reuse protocols that explicitly aim to maintain layer uniformity and stable optical absorptivity can reduce run-to-run variations in residual stress, even though the average stress level is often primarily governed by scan strategy and substrate preheating conditions.

sections.heading: Process atmosphere control
paragraphs: Process atmosphere is often regarded primarily as a safety and defect-control parameter, but it also functions as a critical material preparation variable because it governs the evolution of powder surface chemistry during powder handling and throughout the build process inside the LPBF chamber. Key atmospheric parameters, including residual oxygen concentration, gas composition, flow regime, and humidity, collectively influence oxidation, nitriding, spatter formation, and laser plume stability. These factors subsequently affect the thermal history of the build and the resulting residual stress distribution. Titanium alloys provide a representative example of this coupling between atmosphere and material behavior. Oxygen uptake in both powder and fabricated components is highly sensitive to residual oxygen levels and heat accumulation during processing. Pauzon et al. demonstrated that oxygen pickup during LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V can be effectively mitigated by reducing residual oxygen levels and limiting thermal accumulation through process-time management, highlighting the direct coupling between atmospheric conditions, thermal history, and material state evolution [ 161 ].

More broadly, Brown et al. reviewed the state of the art in atmosphere control for LPBF and noted that atmosphere management systems are evolving from passive inerting
strategies toward actively controlled, closed-loop systems [ 162 ]. Such developments are particularly relevant for stabilizing process conditions and ensuring consistent residual stress outcomes in industrial production environments [ 160 ]. For austenitic and nitrogen-alloyed stainless steels, nitrogen-based atmospheres may offer advantages from both cost and compositional perspectives. However, they can also influence nitride formation and nitrogen uptake, thereby affecting microstructure development and indirectly influencing residual stress through modifications to yield strength and thermal strain partitioning. Pauzon et al. compared argon and nitrogen processing atmospheres for LPBF of 316L stainless steel and reported measurable differences in porosity and residual stress, emphasizing the importance of gas selection [ 163 ]. Similarly, Mirz et al. investigated nitrogen-alloyed grades such as AISI 318LN and quantified the influence of processing atmosphere on microstructure and mechanical properties, highlighting the need to align atmosphere selection with alloy chemistry and targeted stress states [ 164 ]. For nickel-based superalloys, atmospheric composition also plays a critical role in determining process stability and spatter behavior. For instance, Deckers et al. reported that oxygen concentration in the processing atmosphere is a dominant factor governing spatter oxidation during LPBF of Alloy 718, which in turn affects both process stability and final component properties [ 165 ]. Consequently, process atmosphere should be regarded as a key operational variable in LPBF. Careful control of atmospheric conditions during fabrication is essential for achieving stable material composition, controlled microstructure evolution, and consistent residual stress levels in the final components.

sections.heading: Transformation engineering through alloy design
paragraphs: Phase transformation engineering has long been employed in low-transformation-temperature (LTT) welding and is increasingly explored in metal additive manufacturing as a strategy to reduce tensile residual stress without relying solely on mechanical post-processing. By carefully designing alloy compositions, solid-state phase transformations during cooling in the LPBF process can introduce transformation strain and transformation plasticity that partially offset thermally induced tensile stresses. This concept has been demonstrated in directed energy deposition using LTT pre-alloyed powders. For example, Chen et al. showed that the austenite-to-martensite transformation occurring during cooling can introduce compressive stresses and thereby reduce net tensile residual stress in the deposited material [ 166 ].

A similar strategy can be applied in LPBF of steels, where martensitic transformation occurs during rapid cooling, particularly in martensitic tool steels and precipitation-hardening grades. A representative LPBF example is 17-4 PH stainless steel, in which the composition-dependent phase balance and martensite start temperature significantly influence residual stress evolution. An et al. proposed an alloy-equivalent phase prediction framework that adjusts the Cr/Ni ratio and energy density to control both the fraction and timing of martensitic transformation. Under suitable conditions, the transformation strain associated with martensite formation can effectively offset thermally induced tensile stresses [ 167 ]. Complementary work by Moyle et al. further correlated microstructure, mechanical properties, and residual stress in LPBF-fabricated 17-4 PH stainless steel, highlighting the critical role of phase constitution and microstructural state in determining the final stress distribution [ 168 ]. It should be noted that not all phase transformations necessarily promote stress mitigation. In Ti-6Al-4V, for instance, the β to α′ martensitic transformation induces a volume change and alters the yield strength of the material. While this transformation can relax or redistribute residual stresses, it does not necessarily convert tensile stresses into compressive stresses. Chen et al. demonstrated through coupled thermo-metallurgical–mechanical modeling that neglecting solid-state transformation strain leads to substantial overprediction of residual stress in SLM Ti-6Al-4V (Fig.  11 b), underscoring the quantitative importance of transformation strain in stress prediction and control [ 169 ]. These findings highlight that alloy selection and post-processing strategies should be carefully aligned with the specific phase transformation pathways of each alloy system to achieve effective residual stress management in LPBF.

sections.heading: Grain refining optimization
paragraphs: Grain refinement represents an effective alloy-level strategy to improve printability and reduce the likelihood of stress-driven cracking and distortion in LPBF. A finer and more equiaxed microstructure generally reduces microstructural anisotropy, enhances ductility at elevated build temperatures, and decreases the sensitivity of the stress state to scan path variations. Although grain refinement does not directly reduce thermal gradients, it facilitates plastic accommodation during cooling and reduces potential crack initiation sites, thereby indirectly stabilizing residual stress and distortion outcomes. Many high-strength aluminum alloys are particularly prone to cracking during LPBF due to their wide solidification ranges and susceptibility to hot tearing. This challenge can be mitigated by introducing inoculants or microalloying additions that promote heterogeneous nucleation and grain refinement. Recent studies have shown that nanoparticle inoculants, such as TiB 2 , TiC, and rare-earth borides, can effectively suppress columnar grain growth, promote equiaxed solidification, and improve processability. These effects can reduce distortion and variability in residual stress by minimizing crack formation and enabling fabrication under lower substrate preheating conditions.

For example, Mair et al. reported that CaB 6  nanoparticles used as inoculants significantly improved the processability and mechanical response of LPBF-fabricated aluminum alloys [ 170 ]. Similarly, Yao et al. employed LaB 6  nanoparticles as grain refiners in 2024 aluminum alloy, achieving significant grain refinement and improved mechanical properties (Fig.  12 a,b) [ 171 ]. Consequently, grain refinement has emerged as an effective strategy for improving the quality of components produced by fusion-based additive manufacturing, particularly for high-strength aluminum alloys that require specially designed inoculation and processing routes [ 172 ]. Across different alloy systems, inoculants are most effective when they remain stable and do not fully dissolve during the thermal cycle, exhibit crystallographic compatibility and low interfacial energy with the nucleating phase, and can be incorporated without compromising powder flowability. In steels and nickel-based alloys, analogous grain refinement approaches may involve microalloying additions or controlled oxide dispersions. However, the design space for these strategies is constrained by segregation behavior, precipitation during rapid solidification, and the feasibility of powder atomization. From the perspective of residual stress management, the practical advantage of grain refinement lies in enabling broader processing windows and reducing the need for extreme substrate preheating, rather than directly lowering the peak magnitude of tensile residual stresses. By improving microstructural stability and ductility during solidification and cooling, inoculant-assisted microstructures can indirectly mitigate stress accumulation and reduce the risk of distortion or cracking during LPBF fabrication.
