sections.heading: Compositional tailoring
paragraphs: For multi-material LPBF, composition gradients can be deliberately engineered to reduce residual stresses at dissimilar-metal interfaces by smoothing transitions in key thermo-physical properties, such as the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) and thermal conductivity. For example, Qu et al. demonstrated the fabrication of full-composition Cu–Ni gradient alloys using micro-LPBF. In their work, a dual-gradient design incorporating both structural and compositional gradients was employed, enabling the adjustment of mechanical properties while achieving smooth compositional transitions across the component. This approach highlights the potential for designing multi-material structures with complex geometries and multifunctional capabilities (Fig.  12 c) [ 173 ]. Further studies have shown that process modifications can also improve compositional homogeneity in multi-material LPBF. Schmidt et al. reported that layer-wise remelting during the build process enhances elemental mixing and reduces abrupt property discontinuities, thereby improving interfacial integrity and reducing residual stresses at material boundaries [ 174 ]. However, in-situ alloying may also introduce additional sources of residual stress if not carefully controlled. Potential issues include unmelted elemental particles, local chemical segregation, and the formation of brittle intermetallic phases, all of which may hinder stress relaxation and promote crack initiation. Consequently, successful stress-oriented in-situ alloying strategies typically require carefully designed powder blending protocols that maintain adequate powder flowability, optimized process parameters that promote melt-pool mixing while avoiding keyhole instability, and appropriate post-build heat treatments to homogenize composition and relieve microsegregation-induced stress gradients.

In summary, material-level strategies for residual stress mitigation in LPBF can be broadly categorized as follows. First, powder condition should be treated as a critical residual stress control variable by implementing stricter reuse standards aimed at maintaining layer uniformity and stable optical absorptivity rather than focusing solely on sustainability considerations. Second, the process atmosphere should be tightly controlled with high purity and low humidity to preserve powder surface chemistry and reduce spatter oxidation, particularly for reactive or nitrogen-sensitive alloys. Third, transformation engineering can be exploited in suitable alloy systems to introduce transformation-induced strain that offsets tensile stresses during cooling. Fourth, inoculants and grain refinement strategies can suppress cracking and enhance plastic accommodation, thereby stabilizing distortion and reducing stress variability. Finally, for multi-material LPBF, in-situ alloying and compositional gradients can be employed to tailor thermo-physical properties and mitigate CTE mismatch at dissimilar-metal interfaces, provided that chemical homogeneity and microstructural stability are carefully maintained.

sections.heading: Post-treatment management of residual stress
paragraphs: In addition to residual stress mitigation through LPBF process parameter optimization and raw material quality control, post-treatment represents another critical approach for managing residual stresses in additively manufactured components. Post-treatment processes not only relieve or eliminate residual stresses but can also actively tailor the stress distribution within the material, thereby preserving geometric accuracy while simultaneously enhancing material performance, including fatigue life, wear resistance, and resistance to stress-corrosion cracking. In this section, key post-treatment strategies are summarized, encompassing thermal treatments, mechanical treatments, and hybrid approaches. Their effectiveness in residual stress management, as well as their influence on microstructure evolution and surface integrity, are systematically examined. In addition, the applicability of these methods across different alloy systems and component geometries is discussed, providing practical guidance for selecting and optimizing post-treatment strategies for residual stress control in LPBF-fabricated components.

sections.heading: Stress relief heat-treatment
paragraphs: During stress-relief heat treatment of LPBF-manufactured components, both of the aforementioned mechanisms operate throughout the process. Residual stresses generated during LPBF often approach or even exceed the room-temperature yield strength of the fabricated alloys [ 177 ,  178 – 179 ]. As the temperature increases during the heating stage, the yield strength decreases and may fall below the residual stress level, thereby inducing plastic deformation and enabling stress redistribution. Once the holding stage is reached, the residual stress is typically reduced to a level below the high-temperature yield strength, and the contribution of stress redistribution becomes less dominant. At this stage, further reduction of residual stress is primarily governed by high-temperature creep deformation and the associated stress relaxation mechanisms.

The key parameters in stress-relief heat treatment are temperature and holding time. Although higher temperatures and longer treatment durations generally promote more effective residual stress reduction, they may also trigger undesirable microstructural changes, such as the formation of detrimental phases or the coarsening of grains and second-phase particles [ 180 ,  181 – 182 ]. Consequently, the optimization of stress-relief heat treatment must carefully balance effective stress relaxation with the prevention of harmful microstructural evolution [ 175 ]. In LPBF-fabricated materials, the metastable microstructures formed during rapid solidification differ substantially from those produced through conventional manufacturing processes [ 183 ,  184 – 185 ]. As a result, stress-relief heat treatment schedules for additively manufactured components often require specific adjustment to accommodate these unique microstructural characteristics. Furthermore, variations in alloy composition, as-built microstructure, mechanical properties, and intended service conditions necessitate material-specific heat treatment strategies. The following sections review representative stress-relief heat treatment schedules for different categories of additively manufactured alloys, highlighting their distinct characteristics and application requirements.

sections.heading: Aluminum-based alloys
paragraphs: Stress-relief annealing [ 186 ,  187 – 188 ], T6 heat treatment [ 189 ,  190 ], and direct aging are the primary thermal treatments used for residual stress mitigation in aluminum alloys [ 191 ,  192 ,  193 – 194 ]. Stress-relief annealing of aluminum alloys is typically conducted at approximately 300 °C for 2–3 h. In contrast, T6 heat treatment involves a solution treatment stage at around 500 °C followed by artificial aging at a lower temperature (typically around 200 °C) for an extended period. However, in LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg, the continuous eutectic silicon network present in the as-built microstructure is disrupted during conventional stress-relief annealing or T6 heat treatment [ 186 ,  187 ,  188 ,  189 – 190 ]. Although these treatments effectively reduce residual stress, they also lead to significant degradation in mechanical strength. To address this issue, Zhang et al. [ 191 ] and Wang et al. [ 195 ] reported that direct aging heat treatments below 200 °C can enhance the mechanical properties of LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg while avoiding the formation of detrimental microstructures. This strengthening effect is attributed to the precipitation of fine second-phase particles during low-temperature aging.

Nevertheless, microstructural stability becomes increasingly sensitive as the temperature rises. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) results indicate that interdiffusion of Si in the Al matrix becomes activated at approximately 227 °C, initiating degradation of the eutectic silicon network (Fig.  13 a) [ 191 ]. Further heating above about 288 °C results in severe disintegration of the eutectic network and the formation of spherical Si particles (Fig.  13 b), which leads to a pronounced reduction in strength [ 186 ,  193 ]. Therefore, to preserve the eutectic silicon network, aging temperatures must be carefully controlled. However, lower treatment temperatures also reduce the efficiency of residual stress relaxation. As shown in the contour maps of microhardness and residual stress reduction rate under different aging temperatures and holding times (Fig.  13 c,d), achieving complete stress relief without compromising mechanical performance remains challenging [ 193 ]. At present, the international standard ASTM F3301 recommends two stress-relief heat treatment schedules for additively manufactured AlSi10Mg alloys: 285 °C for 2 h and 190 °C for 2 h (Table  1 ). Based on the preceding discussion, the former schedule provides more effective residual stress relief but leads to some degradation in mechanical properties, whereas the latter better preserves the as-built mechanical performance but results in less complete stress removal. Therefore, the selection of these heat treatment schedules should be determined according to the specific requirements of the intended application. Although extensive research has been conducted on post-treatment strategies for LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloys, studies focusing on stress-relief heat treatment for other emerging high-strength or heat-resistant aluminum alloys remain relatively limited. Consequently, systematic investigations into optimized stress-relief heat treatment schedules for different aluminum alloy systems are still required to support their broader adoption in additive manufacturing applications.

sections.heading: Titanium-based alloys
paragraphs: For Ti-6Al-4V, one of the most widely used titanium alloys, conventional stress-relief heat treatments are typically performed at 480–650 °C for 1–4 h [ 196 ,  197 ]. In LPBF-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V, the as-built microstructure is dominated by acicular α′ martensite, which begins to decompose into equilibrium α and β phases at temperatures above approximately 400 °C [ 198 ]. Consequently, stress-relief heat treatment of LPBF Ti-6Al-4V is generally accompanied by phase transformation processes. Haar et al. [ 199 ] investigated stress-relief annealing of LPBF-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V at different temperatures and reported that annealing at 480 °C and 560 °C for 1 h did not reduce the strength of the material. Instead, an increase in strength was observed, with a more pronounced strengthening effect occurring at the lower annealing temperature (Fig.  14 a,b). This strengthening behavior was attributed to the formation of ultrafine vanadium-rich β precipitates and a transitional α phase with an anisotropic hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice structure during the phase transformation induced by lower-temperature heat treatment (Fig.  14 c) [ 198 ,  199 – 200 ]. However, the precipitation of β phase and the formation of transitional α structures may also increase the brittleness of the material. Meanwhile, the effectiveness of residual stress relief increases with annealing temperature. Annealing at 560 °C for 1 h or higher has been reported to relieve approximately 90% of the residual stress. Although higher annealing temperatures can partially mitigate the embrittlement associated with β precipitation, they are typically accompanied by a reduction in strength (Fig.  14 a,b). Reproduced with permission from [ 199 ]. Copyright 2020 Wiley.  c  Microstructure and corresponding schematic of α′/α structural evolution. Reproduced with permission from  [ 198 ,  200 ]. Copyright 2020 and 2021 Elsevier

To achieve high strength and adequate ductility at room temperature, Ti-6Al-4V should ideally exhibit an α + β dual-phase microstructure [ 201 ]. However, Ti-6Al-4V fabricated by LPBF predominantly presents an acicular α′ martensitic microstructure in the as-built state, which leads to high strength but insufficient elongation [ 202 ,  203 – 204 ]. Therefore, post-fabrication heat treatment is generally required to transform the martensitic structure into the desired α + β dual-phase microstructure. Under this consideration, employing higher-temperature stress-relief annealing is often acceptable, even though it may be accompanied by some reduction in strength. For example, Frkan et al. applied stress-relief annealing at 740 °C and 900 °C to LPBF-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V [ 205 ]. Their results showed that the lamellar α + β dual-phase microstructure obtained after treatment at 900 °C exhibited significantly improved elongation and fatigue strength compared with the microstructure treated at 740 °C, which still retained a portion of the acicular martensite. Nevertheless, when adopting higher stress-relief temperatures, care must be taken to avoid excessively high temperatures that may lead to grain coarsening and coarsening of the lamellar α + β microstructure. When the temperature exceeds approximately 1000 °C, the α or α′ phase completely transforms into the β phase, resulting in a single-phase β microstructure [ 206 ,  207 ]. Under such conditions, the prior-β grains become highly susceptible to significant coarsening [ 208 ,  209 ], which can degrade mechanical performance. Therefore, high-temperature stress-relief heat treatments are generally recommended to be conducted below the β-transus temperature.

In addition to the aforementioned stress-relief heat treatment strategies involving phase transformation, Xiao et al. investigated a low-temperature stress-relief treatment at 350 °C, which is below the martensite decomposition temperature [ 210 ]. Their results showed that a holding time of more than 10 h is required to achieve near-complete stress relief, with approximately 86% of the residual stress reduced after 10 h of treatment. Compared with medium-temperature stress-relief annealing at 650 °C, which typically requires only about 0.5 h to achieve nearly complete stress removal, the duration of the low-temperature annealing process is nearly 20 times longer [ 35 ]. According to the international standard F3301, a medium-temperature stress-relief schedule of 593 °C for 2 h is recommended for additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V (Table  1 ). Although this treatment may involve a slight reduction in ductility, subsequent solution treatment and aging can effectively restore and even enhance ductility. Ultimately, this combined treatment enables the formation of a well-balanced α + β dual-phase microstructure, achieving a desirable strength-ductility synergy [ 209 ].

For commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti), which is a single α-phase alloy, the as-built microstructure produced under the rapid solidification conditions of the LPBF process is predominantly composed of acicular α′ martensite [ 211 ]. During subsequent stress-relief heat treatment, the process typically involves the decomposition of martensite into the equilibrium α phase, which may also be accompanied by recrystallization [ 212 ,  213 ]. Han et al. investigated the stress-relief annealing behavior of LPBF-fabricated CP-Ti within the temperature range of 490–890 °C with a holding time of 2 h [ 214 ]. Their results showed that residual stress gradually decreased with increasing annealing temperature. At 590 °C, recrystallization occurred, leading to an approximately 80% reduction in residual stress (Fig.  15 a). Due to the combined effects of α′ martensite decomposition and recrystallization, the yield strength decreased by about 10%, while the elongation improved to some extent (Fig.  15 b,c). When the annealing temperature exceeded the α to β transformation temperature (882 °C) and reached 890 °C, the residual stress was further reduced to approximately 90% lower than that of the as-built state [ 215 ]. However, this condition also resulted in a significant decrease in yield strength of approximately 25%. Considering that annealing above the phase transformation temperature does not substantially improve residual stress relief but causes considerable strength degradation, stress-relief heat treatment above the β-transus temperature is generally not recommended. At present, the international standard F3301 recommends a stress-relief heat treatment schedule of 593 °C for 2 h for additively manufactured CP-Ti. Copyright 2023 Elsevier

For near-β titanium alloys, such as Ti–5Al–5Mo–5V–1Cr–1Fe, the conventional microstructure primarily consists of a β-matrix with a small fraction of precipitated α phase [ 216 ,  217 ]. However, under the rapid cooling conditions characteristic of the LPBF process, the precipitation of the α phase is largely suppressed, resulting in an as-built microstructure composed predominantly of metastable β phase [ 218 ]. During subsequent stress-relief heat treatment, precipitation of the α phase typically occurs, which can significantly strengthen LPBF-fabricated Ti–5Al–5Mo–5V–1Cr–1Fe alloys. For example, Shaha et al. applied a stress-relief heat treatment schedule commonly used for conventionally processed material (850 °C for 4 h) [ 218 ]. This treatment eliminated 62–91% of the residual stress and increased the yield strength by approximately 22%, although a slight reduction in elongation was observed. At present, the effectiveness of lower-temperature stress-relief treatments for Ti–5Al–5Mo–5V–1Cr–1Fe remains unclear. However, according to Zhang et al., aging heat treatment at 600 °C or below can induce the precipitation of acicular α′ martensite or ω phase, which may lead to severe embrittlement in this alloy [ 219 ]. Therefore, stress-relief heat treatment below 600 °C is generally not recommended for Ti–5Al–5Mo–5V–1Cr–1Fe. Currently, unified process specifications and standards for stress-relief heat treatment of near-β titanium alloys remain lacking. Overall, stress-relief heat treatment of LPBF-fabricated titanium alloys typically involves the transformation of acicular α′ martensite or supersaturated β phase into equilibrium α and β phases. Consequently, an appropriate heat-treatment schedule must be carefully selected to achieve effective stress relief while avoiding excessive microstructural coarsening or the formation of detrimental phases.

sections.heading: Iron-based alloys
paragraphs: The as-built microstructure of 316L stainless steel fabricated by LPBF primarily consists of a single-phase FCC matrix containing a cellular substructure with a high density of entangled dislocations [ 220 ,  221 – 222 ]. This unique cellular architecture imparts higher strength and ductility compared with conventionally processed 316L stainless steel [ 223 ,  224 – 225 ]. However, these cellular structures are highly susceptible to recovery and recrystallization during annealing, which can degrade their characteristic microstructural features [ 226 ,  227 ]. Therefore, for LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel, the objective is typically to identify a stress-relief heat-treatment schedule that effectively reduces residual stress while preserving the cellular substructure as much as possible. According to the study by Chao et al., the cellular structure of LPBF-fabricated 316L remained largely preserved after low-temperature annealing at 400 °C, although the residual stress was reduced by only 23% [ 228 ]. In contrast, higher annealing temperatures (≥ 650 °C) resulted in more substantial stress relief (> 63%), but also caused degradation of the cellular structure, σ-phase precipitation, and grain growth, ultimately leading to decreased strength and ductility (Fig.  16 a–c). Similarly, An et al. reported that even a short annealing treatment of 10 min at 650 °C induced pronounced dislocation recovery and blurring of cell walls, while the residual stress remained nearly unchanged [ 229 ]. These findings indicate that it is challenging to effectively relieve residual stress while simultaneously maintaining the high strength and ductility characteristic of the as-built state through conventional stress-relief annealing. Reproduced with permission from [ 228 ], Copyright 2021 Elsevier.  d  Cellular structure evolution in 316H stainless steel after holding at 650 °C for different durations. Reproduced with permission from  [ 233 ]. Copyright 2023 Elsevier

The international standard F3301 does not specifically address the preservation of the cellular substructure in LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel. Instead, it recommends a two-step stress-relief heat treatment strategy consisting of a high-temperature step followed by a low-temperature holding stage of 899 °C for 0.5–1 h, followed by 371 °C for 0.5–1 h (Table  1 ). The selection of 899 °C primarily aims to achieve effective stress relief while avoiding the sensitization temperature range of stainless steels (500–850 °C). This approach prevents prolonged exposure within this temperature window, which could otherwise promote extensive chromium-rich carbide precipitation along grain boundaries, leading to chromium depletion near the boundaries and degradation of corrosion resistance [ 230 ,  231 – 232 ]. The subsequent low-temperature holding stage is intended to eliminate secondary residual stresses that may arise from non-uniform cooling or phase transformations during the high-temperature treatment, thereby further improving dimensional stability. In comparison, LPBF-fabricated 316H stainless steel exhibits higher thermal stability of its cellular structure than 316L, with the cellular architecture remaining largely intact even after 6 h of annealing at 650 °C (Fig.  16 d) [ 233 ,  234 ]. However, annealing at this temperature may promote carbide precipitation. To balance residual stress relief with microstructural stability, Kumari et al. recommended a stress-relief annealing schedule of 650 °C for 2 h for LPBF-produced 316H stainless steel, which can effectively reduce residual stress while minimizing microstructural degradation associated with carbide precipitation [ 233 ].

Another austenitic stainless steel 21-6-9 fabricated by LPBF also exhibits a cellular substructure in the as-built state [ 235 ]. Studies have shown that its strength gradually decreases with increasing annealing temperature, although the reduction remains modest and is not accompanied by a significant loss of ductility. Even after annealing at 800 °C, where residual stresses are almost completely relieved, the cellular structure remains observable, and the yield strength decreases by only approximately 13% compared with the as-built condition. For the precipitation-strengthened martensitic stainless steel 18Ni300 maraging steel, the microstructure produced by LPBF consists primarily of acicular martensite, lacking the strengthening intermetallic precipitates required for optimal performance [ 236 ,  237 ]. To fully unlock the material’s strengthening potential, aging heat treatment is typically applied after fabrication to promote the precipitation of intermetallic compounds and achieve significant strengthening (Fig.  17 a) [ 238 ,  239 – 240 ]. However, although aging effectively modifies the microstructure and improves mechanical properties such as tensile strength and hardness, its ability to relieve residual stress is limited. Santos et al. reported that the residual stress in aged specimens remained at approximately 70% of the level in as-built samples [ 241 ]. Therefore, additional post-heat-treatment processes are required to effectively reduce residual stress in LPBF-fabricated 18Ni300 maraging steel. For example, Shan et al. introduced an annealing step at 820 °C for 1 h prior to aging treatment (490 °C for 5 h) [ 242 ]. Their results demonstrated that this combined heat-treatment strategy achieved nearly complete residual stress relief, while causing only a marginal reduction in overall mechanical performance compared with direct aging alone (Fig.  17 b–d). In summary, for LPBF-fabricated austenitic stainless steels strengthened by cellular substructures, the design of stress-relief heat treatment schedules should aim to preserve the cellular architecture as much as possible, since it plays a crucial role in maintaining the superior strength-ductility combination of the as-built material. For precipitation-strengthened martensitic stainless steels, which require post-fabrication heat treatment to achieve their designed mechanical performance, stress-relief annealing itself generally does not severely degrade the microstructure. However, the annealing schedule must still avoid excessively high temperatures to prevent coarsening of the prior-austenite grains, which would otherwise compromise the overall mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Nickel-based alloys
paragraphs: For LPBF-fabricated nickel-based superalloys, a notable distinction exists in the design of stress-relief heat treatments between solid-solution-strengthened and precipitation-strengthened systems. Solid-solution-strengthened superalloys generally exhibit good ductility but relatively lower strength, which allows effective stress relief to be achieved at comparatively lower temperatures. Similar to the alloy systems discussed above, the design of stress-relief heat-treatment schedules for these alloys must also avoid the formation of detrimental secondary phases. For example, the recommended stress-relief heat-treatment schedule for LPBF-fabricated IN625 alloy is 800 °C for 1 h [ 243 ,  244 ]. This temperature is lower than the 870 °C typically recommended for wrought IN625 [ 245 ,  246 ]. The reduction in treatment temperature primarily arises from the microsegregation of Nb and Mo in interdendritic regions that commonly occurs in LPBF-fabricated IN625. Such segregation significantly increases the tendency for δ-phase precipitation during stress-relief annealing compared with conventionally processed materials [ 247 ,  248 – 249 ]. The formation of the δ phase is known to degrade ductility and reduce creep resistance [ 243 ,  250 ,  251 ]. To suppress this undesirable precipitation behavior, a lower stress-relief temperature of 800 °C is employed for LPBF-produced IN625. This schedule achieves stress-relief effectiveness comparable to the 870 °C treatment used for wrought components, resulting in nearly complete elimination of residual stress (Fig.  18 ) [ 243 ,  244 ]. Reproduced with permission from  [ 244 ].  Copyright 2017 Springer Nature

Kangazian et al. applied a stress-relief annealing treatment at 900 °C for 2 h to LPBF-fabricated Hastelloy X, a solid-solution-strengthened nickel-based superalloy designed for service temperatures up to 900 °C, but observed a noticeable reduction in ductility [ 252 ]. This deterioration was attributed to the decomposition of the originally strengthening granular M 6 C carbides and the precipitation of brittle M 23 C 6  carbides along grain boundaries at this temperature [ 253 ]. Previous studies indicate that within the temperature range of 760–980 °C, M 6 C carbides continuously decompose while M 23 C 6  carbides precipitate [ 254 ,  255 ]. Prolonged holding within this temperature window leads to excessive consumption of finely dispersed M 6 C carbides, which contribute to precipitation strengthening, while simultaneously promoting the formation of brittle M 23 C 6  carbides at grain boundaries, thereby degrading both high-temperature and room-temperature mechanical properties [ 256 ,  257 ]. Although M 23 C 6  carbides can redissolve at temperatures above 980 °C, accompanied by the reprecipitation of M 6 C, the original dispersion-strengthening effect cannot be fully restored. Therefore, the optimal stress-relief temperature range for Hastelloy X should either be below 760 °C or above 980 °C, in order to avoid the undesirable transformation of M 6 C to M 23 C 6 . At present, most studies on LPBF-fabricated Hastelloy X directly adopt the standard solution heat-treatment schedule of 1175–1180 °C for 2 h [ 258 ]. This treatment not only effectively relieves residual stress, but also promotes microstructural homogenization and allows control of grain-boundary carbide morphology during cooling, thereby achieving an overall optimization of microstructure and mechanical performance [ 259 ].

Precipitation-strengthened nickel-based superalloys, in contrast, possess higher strength and excellent high-temperature performance. Due to their high residual stress levels and strong microstructural stability, low-temperature heat treatments are often insufficient to achieve effective stress relief. Consequently, higher annealing temperatures, typically close to or above the dissolution temperature of the strengthening phases, are commonly required. For example, in LPBF-fabricated GH4099 alloy, residual stress is nearly completely relieved only when the stress-relief annealing temperature is increased to approximately 1000 °C [ 260 ]. This behavior is clearly demonstrated by the distortion measurements of specimens annealed at different temperatures (Fig.  19 a). Considering that the complete dissolution temperature of the γ′ strengthening phase in GH4099 is approximately 975 °C (Fig.  19 b) [ 261 ], an effective stress-relief heat-treatment temperature should therefore be set close to the γ′ dissolution temperature. Some studies, however, have employed stress-relief heat-treatment temperatures significantly below the γ′ dissolution temperature. For instance, Messé et al. reported the use of 840 °C for 24 h for LPBF-fabricated IN738LC alloy, which is considerably lower than its γ′ dissolution temperature of approximately 1160 °C [ 262 ,  263 – 264 ]. Although the actual stress-relief effectiveness at this temperature was not evaluated, the study reported that such low-temperature treatment promoted γ′ precipitation and transformed primary MC carbides into brittle secondary M 23 C 6  carbides along grain boundaries, which may adversely affect the mechanical properties. For alloys such as IN738LC, which contain a high volume fraction of γ′ phase (> 50%), low-temperature heat treatment can lead to extensive precipitation of both γ′ and M 23 C 6  carbides [ 265 ,  266 ]. This process introduces significant phase-transformation stresses that superimpose on the inherent residual stresses generated during the LPBF process, potentially resulting in cracking, as reported by Miao et al. [ 267 ] and Ning et al. [ 268 ]. Therefore, heat-treatment temperatures far below the γ′ dissolution temperature are generally not recommended for heavily γ′-strengthened superalloys. This limitation arises not only because the precipitation of γ′ at low temperatures hinders effective stress relief, but also because it significantly increases the risk of cracking. In conventional welding of such alloys, a common strategy is rapid heating to temperatures close to or above the complete dissolution temperature of the γ′ phase, thereby suppressing excessive γ′ precipitation during stress-relief treatment and improving the effectiveness of residual stress reduction.

For another precipitation-strengthened superalloy IN718, the primary strengthening phase is γ″, rather than the γ′ phase found in alloys such as IN738LC, IN939, and GH4099, and its typical service temperature is correspondingly lower than that of γ′-strengthened counterparts [ 269 ,  270 ]. According to the international standard F3055, the recommended stress-relief heat treatment for LPBF-fabricated IN718 is 1065 °C for 1.5 h. Gruber et al. applied this recommended schedule to LPBF-fabricated IN718 stator vanes and observed negligible distortion, demonstrating that the process enables component-level, shape-preserving stress relief (Fig.  19 c) [ 271 ]. This treatment temperature exceeds not only the dissolution temperature of the Laves phase, but also the precipitation temperatures of δ, γ′, and γ″ phases (Fig.  19 d) [ 272 ,  273 – 274 ]. Such a design provides several advantages. First, it prevents premature precipitation of the γ′ and γ″ phases strengthening phases during heat treatment, thereby avoiding obstruction to stress relaxation. Second, it effectively eliminates the non-equilibrium Laves phase formed during additive manufacturing (Fig.  19 d,e) and suppresses the formation of detrimental δ phase during annealing [ 275 ,  276 – 277 ]. However, at such elevated temperatures, grain boundaries are insufficiently pinned by second-phase particles, making recrystallization and grain growth highly likely [ 278 ,  279 ]. Therefore, the holding time at this temperature must be carefully controlled to ensure adequate residual stress relief while preventing excessive grain coarsening.

In summary, stress-relief heat treatment for LPBF-fabricated alloys must be tailored according to their as-built microstructural characteristics, phase-transformation behavior, and intended performance requirements. An effective heat-treatment schedule should fully alleviate residual stresses while avoiding the formation of detrimental phases or undesirable microstructural degradation, thereby ensuring dimensional stability without sacrificing mechanical properties. Looking forward, future studies should further integrate multi-scale microstructural characterization, thermodynamic analysis, and process simulation to establish more systematic and predictive stress-relief design frameworks for additively manufactured materials. Such efforts will facilitate the development of material-specific heat-treatment guidelines, enabling more reliable performance and broader industrial adoption of LPBF-fabricated components.

sections.heading: Deep cryogenic treatment
paragraphs: In addition to conventional heat-treatment methods, several alternative post-processing techniques, such as deep cryogenic treatment (DCT), cryogenic thermal cycling treatment, and thermal vibration stress relief (TSVR), have been explored for relieving residual stress in LPBF-fabricated components while minimizing microstructural changes associated with high-temperature treatments. DCT is a thermal processing technique in which a material is held at ultralow temperatures (typically below −150 °C, commonly using liquid nitrogen at −196 °C) for an extended period, followed by a controlled return to room temperature [ 280 ,  281 ]. This process operates on the principle of “using cold instead of heat,” where non-uniform thermal contraction induced by extreme low temperatures acts as the driving force. Such contraction can trigger localized plastic deformation at the microscale, thereby relaxing and redistributing residual stresses [ 282 ,  283 – 284 ]. A key advantage of this treatment is its ability to effectively reduce residual stress without significantly altering the original microstructural morphology of the material. Consequently, it is particularly suitable for microstructure-sensitive components or for applications where the unique substructures generated during additive manufacturing, such as cellular architectures, must be preserved.

For example, Zhou et al. [ 285 ] applied DCT to relieve residual stress in LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy. They reported that after cryogenic exposure at −196 °C for 24 h, the residual stress was reduced by 72.7%, which is comparable to the stress-relief effect achieved by conventional solution treatment at 500 °C for 2 h followed by aging at 170 °C for 6 h. Because cryogenic treatment does not induce dislocation recovery or decomposition of metastable microstructures, both the strength and elongation of the cryogenically treated samples remained essentially unchanged. In contrast, the yield strength of the heat-treated samples decreased by approximately 43% compared with the as-built condition. Furthermore, Tang et al. combined cryogenic treatment with low-temperature aging by proposing a cryogenic–thermal cycling strategy, consisting of holding at −160 °C for 1 h followed by heating to 160 °C for 1 h [ 286 ,  287 ]. After three cycles, the residual stress in LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy was reduced by 71%, comparable to the stress-relief effect obtained through prolonged single-step cryogenic treatment. Compared with the single cryogenic process, this cycling method not only provides higher stress-relief efficiency but also preserves the as-built eutectic silicon network while promoting the precipitation of nanoscale phases, resulting in significant strengthening of the LPBF-produced AlSi10Mg alloy. Nevertheless, DCT is not suitable for materials with poor low-temperature ductility. Moreover, the underlying stress-relief mechanism, which relies on differential thermal contraction between phases, has inherent limitations. The thermal contraction stresses generated during the cryogenic process may themselves introduce additional internal stresses, potentially posing challenges for achieving and maintaining high-precision dimensional stability in the final components.

sections.heading: Vibration stress relief treatment
paragraphs: Vibration stress relief (VSR) is a green post-processing technique in which periodic mechanical vibrations are applied to a component to induce microplastic flow under cyclic loading, thereby reducing and redistributing residual stresses [ 288 ,  289 ]. VSR offers several advantages, including no thermal impact on the material, low energy consumption, and high operational efficiency. However, its practical application is limited by relatively low stress-relief effectiveness and uneven stress redistribution across the component [ 290 ,  291 ,  292 – 293 ]. To overcome these limitations, TVSR has been developed [ 294 ,  295 ,  296 – 297 ]. This hybrid technique combines the benefits of thermal stress relief (TSR) and VSR into a coupled thermo-mechanical process. In TVSR, the component is first heated to a predetermined temperature, after which mechanical vibration at a specified frequency and duration is applied during the holding stage. Through this synergistic thermo-mechanical action, residual stresses can be relieved more efficiently and uniformly.

For example, in LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy, TVSR conducted at 175 °C achieved a residual stress reduction of 65.52%, representing improvements of 35% and 91% compared with TSR and VSR at the same temperature, respectively [ 298 ]. Similarly, for Ti-6Al-4V alloy, TVSR performed at 380 °C resulted in a stress-relief rate of 86.76%, which is 76% and 63.63% higher than that achieved by standalone TSR and VSR processes, respectively [ 299 ]. This coupled thermo-mechanical approach not only overcomes the limited stress-relief capability of pure vibration treatment, but also enables effective stress reduction at relatively low temperatures, thereby minimizing the risk of microstructural degradation associated with prolonged high-temperature exposure. Nevertheless, despite partially addressing the limitations of conventional vibration treatment, thermal-vibration coupled processing remains inherently a localized energy-input method. For additively manufactured components with complex geometries, internal cavities, or large dimensions, vibration energy may not propagate uniformly throughout the structure, leading to incomplete stress redistribution. As a result, this technique is often more suitable for targeted local treatment of stress-concentration regions, such as support-contact areas, thin-wall junctions, and locations with abrupt geometric transitions, rather than for uniform stress relief across the entire component. In practical engineering applications, these methods are therefore often combined with bulk heat-treatment processes, with the specific strategy determined according to the component geometry and residual stress distribution. Such integration enables the development of hybrid stress-relief strategies that balance processing efficiency, microstructural stability, and dimensional accuracy.

sections.heading: Shot peening
paragraphs: In addition to the aforementioned global stress-relief methods, localized surface modification techniques, such as shot peening and laser shock peening, are also applied to LPBF-fabricated metal components to modify their stress states. Unlike bulk stress-relief approaches, the primary objective of these techniques is not to directly eliminate residual stresses, but rather to introduce a beneficial compressive stress layer in the near-surface region, refine the surface microstructure, and modify surface roughness. These effects can significantly enhance the fatigue resistance, wear performance, and resistance to stress-corrosion cracking of the component. Consequently, such techniques are typically employed as performance-enhancement measures for critical regions, forming a complementary post-processing strategy when combined with global heat-treatment methods [ 300 ,  301 ]. Shot peening is a widely adopted industrial surface-enhancement process [ 15 ,  302 ]. In this mechanical surface-treatment method, high-velocity metallic or ceramic media impact the component surface, inducing plastic deformation within the surface layer and thereby reducing surface defects. This plastic deformation also generates significant compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region, which effectively improves the fatigue resistance and stress-corrosion cracking resistance of the material [ 182 ,  303 ,  304 ].

The effectiveness of shot peening is primarily governed by parameters such as peening coverage, media type, media size, impact angle, and processing time. Zhang et al. systematically investigated the influence of peening coverage [ 304 ], media type [ 305 ], and media size [ 306 ,  307 ] on the surface residual stress of LPBF-fabricated 304L stainless steel. Their results demonstrated that peening coverage is the most influential parameter (Fig.  20 ). When the coverage increased to 450%, the surface compressive stress reached approximately −900 MPa, with an affected depth of 62.25 μm. However, higher compressive surface stress does not necessarily lead to better performance. Excessively high compressive stress is often associated with severe plastic deformation, which may cause surface damage, a phenomenon referred to as over shot peening (OSP). Based on parameters such as Almen intensity and surface coverage, shot peening processes can generally be categorized into conventional shot peening (CSP) and severe shot peening (SSP) (Fig.  21 a) [ 308 ]. This classification provides an important framework for optimizing peening parameters while balancing surface strengthening with damage control. Among the three types of shot peening, SSP is considered the most suitable for the surface treatment of LPBF-fabricated metals. This process can induce nanocrystallization within the near-surface layer and introduce higher and deeper compressive residual stresses, while effectively avoiding the surface damage commonly associated with excessive peening conditions [ 309 ,  310 ]. As a result, SSP demonstrates clear advantages over CSP and OSP in terms of enhancing mechanical properties and fatigue performance. Building upon this concept, Maleki et al. proposed a novel shot-peening strategy termed gradient severe shot peening (GSSP) [ 311 ]. In the GSSP process, varying projection pressures are applied instead of the constant pressure used in conventional peening. The process can be implemented through two primary strategies (Fig.  21 b) including ascending severe shot peening (ASSP) and ascending–descending severe shot peening (ADSSP). This approach aims to avoid the detrimental effects associated with OSP, while fully exploiting the benefits of surface-layer nanocrystallization, strain hardening, and the strengthening effect of high compressive residual stresses.

Furthermore, the researchers extended this technique to LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy, evaluating its applicability and strengthening effects in additively manufactured materials (Fig.  21 c,d) [ 308 ]. Although shot peening can improve the surface roughness of additively manufactured alloys while simultaneously modifying the surface stress state, the degree of improvement is often insufficient to meet direct service requirements. To further enhance surface quality, some researchers have combined shot peening with vibratory surface finishing. This integrated post-processing approach has been shown to reduce surface roughness to approximately 2 μm, while simultaneously increasing the magnitude of compressive residual stress from about −600 MPa after peening to approximately −700 MPa. As a result, the combined treatment leads to significant improvements in mechanical performance, including an approximately 1.5-fold increase in tensile strength and up to a threefold improvement in fatigue life [ 312 ].

sections.heading: Laser shock peening
paragraphs: Laser shock peening (LSP) employs a high-energy pulsed laser to rapidly vaporize a thin water layer covering the component surface, generating an expanding plasma. The resulting plasma-induced shock wave propagates as a compressive stress pulse, which plastically deforms the near-surface region of the component [ 302 ]. This process introduces beneficial compressive residual stresses into the surface layer, thereby enhancing fatigue and damage resistance. Compared with shot peening, LSP typically produces a lower degree of cold work, resulting in greater stability of the induced compressive residual stresses [ 180 ]. In addition, the penetration depth of compressive residual stress generated by LSP is significantly greater, typically reaching around 1 mm, whereas the depth produced by shot peening generally ranges from 0.1 to 0.6 mm [ 313 ]. Another advantage of LSP is its ability to mitigate near-surface porosity-type defects within several hundred micrometers of the surface [ 314 ]. For example, Maleki et al. [ 315 ] reported that, in LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy, LSP was capable of closing near-surface pores at depths of approximately 390–420 μm, resulting in an overall mean porosity reduction of 52% in as-built samples and 62% in heat-treated samples.

Although LSP is not a heat-treatment process intended for surface remelting, high-energy laser pulses may still induce localized surface micro-melting. For example, in investigating LSP without protective coatings on LPBF-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V, Saklakoglu et al. observed that the treatment introduced a maximum compressive residual stress of approximately −850 MPa within a near-surface depth of about 0.5 mm [ 316 ]. However, localized surface micro-melting during the process led to an increase in surface roughness. To mitigate potential thermal damage induced by pulsed laser irradiation, Chen et al. employed aluminum foil as a protective layer during LSP of LPBF surfaces [ 317 ]. Other protective coatings commonly used in LSP processes include polyvinyl chloride (PVC) tape [ 318 ] and black paint [ 319 ]. Nevertheless, even with such protective layers, the high-energy vapor-driven shock waves generated during LSP may still produce impact-induced surface ripples, which can increase surface roughness [ 317 ]. Based on findings reported in multiple studies, even when the pulse energy is carefully controlled and surface remelting is avoided, LSP generally provides negligible improvement in surface roughness [ 302 ,  320 ]. Consequently, LSP is often combined with additional surface-finishing processes to optimize surface quality. For instance, after applying LSP, Maleki et al. performed electrochemical polishing on LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy, further reducing surface roughness and ultimately achieving a 400-fold improvement in fatigue life compared with the as-built condition [ 315 ].

Matusů et al. compared the LSP response of machined and as-built surfaces in LPBF-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy [ 321 ]. Their results showed that machined surfaces exhibited higher compressive residual stress levels and greater stress-affected depths after LSP treatment. This difference is attributed to the high residual tensile stresses typically present on as-built LPBF surfaces, which partially offset the compressive stresses introduced by the LSP-generated vapor shock waves. Machining removes this tensile surface stress layer, enabling LSP to more effectively introduce compressive residual stresses. Since higher compressive stresses are generally beneficial for improving fatigue performance, these findings suggest that surface preparation plays a critical role in maximizing the effectiveness of LSP. Therefore, it is recommended that LSP be applied after bulk stress-relief heat treatment and appropriate surface preparation, in order to achieve optimal residual stress control and fatigue enhancement.

Higher compressive residual stresses can be achieved by increasing the laser pulse energy [ 315 ,  322 ] and raising the pulse density [ 317 ,  323 ]. However, excessively high pulse energy may lead to surface ablation and the formation of re-solidified structures, which degrade surface integrity and consequently have a detrimental impact on fatigue performance [ 322 ]. In contrast, increasing the pulse density generally has a much smaller influence on surface roughness, while still significantly enhancing the magnitude of compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region. For example, Mahar increased the pulse density from 0.5 pulse/mm 2  to 2.5 pulse/mm 2  on machined LPBF-fabricated Scalmalloy specimens, resulting in an increase in the maximum near-surface compressive stress from approximately −300 MPa to about −500 MPa, while the surface roughness remained within the range of 1.8–2.1 μm [ 323 ]. In addition, Ouyang et al. applied a combined LSP and shot peening treatment to LPBF-fabricated IN718 alloy, which significantly enhanced the near-surface compressive stress state [ 324 ]. Compared with LSP alone, the hybrid process increased the maximum compressive residual stress by 68%, while compared with shot peening alone, it extended the depth of the compressive stress field by 112%. This hybrid approach effectively integrates the deep stress penetration capability of LSP with the high surface compressive stress magnitude introduced by shot peening.

In addition to the aforementioned localized post-processing techniques, such as shot peening and LSP, other surface stress-regulation methods have also been explored. For instance, Gu et al. proposed an ultra-high-speed shock (UHSS) approach applied to LPBF-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V alloy, demonstrating its potential for modifying surface stress states and enhancing mechanical performance [ 325 ]. Moreover, other surface-enhancement techniques, including water jet peening, cavitation peening, and ultrasonic nanocrystal surface modification, also exhibit potential application value. However, no systematic studies have reported their application to additively manufactured components to date. Despite their advantages, these surface modification techniques share a common limitation. For additively manufactured components with complex geometries or internal cavities, the accessibility of these processes is often restricted. In addition, when applied to thin-walled structures, the induced plastic deformation may lead to out-of-tolerance distortions, resulting in deviations from the intended geometric shape and dimensional accuracy.

sections.heading: A workflow of low-residual-stress LPBF printing
paragraphs: Residual stress in LPBF is not a single-parameter defect, but the integrated outcome of multiple interacting factors, including thermal history, geometrical constraints, microstructure evolution, and the capacity of the material to accommodate strain during repeated heating and cooling cycles. Therefore, achieving low-residual-stress LPBF manufacturing requires the implementation of a closed-loop workflow that systematically links simulation-based prediction, manufacturing strategy optimization, material-level design, and post-treatment management. Within such a framework, experimental validation and iterative refinement should be incorporated at each stage to continuously improve prediction accuracy and process reliability.

sections.heading: Define application-driven targets
paragraphs: A practical workflow must begin by defining what level of residual stress is acceptable for the intended component, since the optimal mitigation strategy depends on the dominant failure risks, such as distortion, cracking, fatigue, stress corrosion, or machining instability. First, acceptance metrics should be established by specifying requirements such as allowable distortion and dimensional tolerances, crack-free integrity, dimensional stability after support removal, machining allowances, and service performance targets. These requirements should then be translated into quantifiable indicators, such as maximum out-of-plane warpage, allowable curvature, or maximum tensile residual stress within critical regions. Second, stress-critical features and constraints must be identified. This involves marking regions that are typically sensitive to residual stress, such as thin walls, overhangs, sharp geometric transitions, or support-contact zones. Identifying these features helps guide where prediction and mitigation efforts should be concentrated, rather than applying uniform strategies across the entire component. Third, appropriate residual stress and distortion measurement techniques should be selected for verification and data acquisition, enabling experimental feedback that supports model validation and iterative optimization within the workflow.

sections.heading: Decision-oriented modeling and simulation prediction
paragraphs: After establishing the stress mitigation targets, simulation can be employed as a front-end screening tool to reduce trial-and-error and identify the dominant contributors to residual stress for the specific geometry and alloy system. The key principle is to match the modeling fidelity to the decision being made. First, appropriate modeling fidelity should be selected according to the scale and objective of the analysis. Macro-scale (part-scale) modeling can be used to predict Type I residual stresses and global distortion, enabling rapid screening of build orientation, support strategies, and overall scanning rules. For large components, inherent strain or modified inherent strain approaches are commonly adopted to achieve sufficient computational efficiency. Second, meso-scale (track-scale) modeling resolves the melt pool thermal history, thermal gradients, and sensitivity to scanning strategies. The resulting outputs can be condensed into calibrated heat-source parameters, layer-wise inherent strain inputs, or simplified thermal descriptors, which can subsequently be used for macro-scale residual stress prediction. Third, micro-scale modeling should be employed when cracking sensitivity is governed by microstructure, or when Type II and Type III residual stresses and anisotropic constitutive responses significantly influence failure risk. These models are particularly valuable for providing mechanistic insight and alloy-specific guidance, rather than for routine part-scale screening. Next, boundary conditions and key model inputs must be carefully calibrated to ensure consistency with the actual machine and powder conditions. This includes verifying assumptions related to laser absorptivity, convection and radiation boundary conditions, substrate constraints, and temperature-dependent material properties. Finally, the simulation outputs should be translated into actionable design constraints, such as identifying hot spots of high tensile stress and potential distortion directions, assessing scan-vector length sensitivity and regions requiring scan segmentation, determining critical support anchors and thermal pathways, and predicting stress redistribution trends under strategies such as preheating or remelting.

sections.heading: Manufacturing process optimization
paragraphs: At this stage, simulation predictions are translated into actionable machine instructions. The optomization principle is to reduce steep thermal gradients and constraint-induced shrinkage incompatibility, while maintaining high density, productivity, and process repeatability. First, optimize the process parameter window with residual stress considered as a constraint. The optimization should begin from a densification-safe process window, and then be refined using stress-aware criteria. Parameter sets that produce unstable melt pools or defect morphologies should be avoided, as these conditions can amplify local stress concentrations and distortion risks. Second, optimize the scan strategy and scanning sequence. Long continuous scan vectors in stress-sensitive regions should be minimized by segmenting scan lengths, while applying inter-layer scan rotation or island scanning strategies to redistribute shrinkage directions and reduce the accumulation of directional stresses. The scan sequence itself should be treated as a design variable, since the order in which islands or regions are scanned can influence local reheating behavior, constraint buildup, and the resulting residual stress distribution. Third, optimize build orientation, topology design, and support structures. Build orientations should be selected to minimize overhang-induced stress accumulation and to relocate stress-sensitive features away from highly constrained regions. Support structures can serve both as mechanical anchors and thermal pathways, and their density, anchor placement, and removal strategy should be carefully designed to balance distortion control with the risk of removal-induced damage. Where possible, abrupt cross-section transitions should be reduced, and fillets or gradual thickness gradients should be introduced to moderate constraint-induced stress concentrations. Finally, preheating and remelting strategies may be employed when appropriate. These approaches can reduce thermal gradients and lower tensile residual stresses, but their implementation must be carefully balanced against potential effects on microstructure and process productivity.

sections.heading: Material-level optimization
paragraphs: Material and process environmental control plays a critical role in reducing the gap between idealized modeling assumptions and actual manufacturing conditions. Key considerations include the following aspects. First, clear powder reuse protocols should be established, including sieving procedures, refresh ratios, and powder traceability, in order to maintain stable powder packing density, optical absorptivity, melt-pool behavior, and defect probability. Inconsistent powder conditions can increase run-to-run residual stress variability and reduce the reliability of simulation-informed process optimization. Second, process atmosphere parameters such as oxygen concentration, humidity level, and gas flow regime must be carefully controlled to stabilize powder surface chemistry and melt-pool behavior. Proper atmosphere control reduces oxidation-related variability in absorptivity, spatter formation, and defect generation, thereby improving process repeatability and the validity of model calibration. Third, phase transformations and transformation-induced strain accommodation can be utilized to mitigate residual stresses and reduce cracking susceptibility for suitable alloy systems. In addition, grain refinement strategies and inoculant additions can promote more equiaxed microstructures, broaden the processable parameter window, and reduce the risk of stress-driven cracking. Fourth, when compositional modification is employed to improve printability or stress accommodation, strict control over chemical homogeneity and alloy compatibility with post-processing schedules is required.

sections.heading: Post-treatment management
paragraphs: Post-treatment strategies should be selected according to the required stress-relief depth, application requirements, and subsequent manufacturing operations. Stress-relief heat treatment remains the baseline solution for reducing bulk residual stresses, improving dimensional stability prior to machining, and minimizing the risk of stress-driven distortion during support removal. Vibration stress relief and thermal–vibration hybrid methods may be considered when microstructure preservation requirements or dimensional constraints limit the use of conventional heat treatment. However, the effectiveness of these approaches depends strongly on factors such as component geometry, fixturing conditions, and vibration energy transmission efficiency. Surface modification techniques, including shot peening and laser shock peening, can introduce beneficial compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region, thereby enhancing fatigue performance and resistance to environmentally assisted cracking. Nevertheless, these methods have inherent limitations, including restricted accessibility for components with internal cavities and the risk of out-of-tolerance deformation in thin-wall structures. Consequently, they are most effective when applied after bulk stress stabilization, serving as complementary surface-strengthening treatments rather than primary stress-relief methods.

sections.heading: Validation, feedback, and qualification to close the loop
paragraphs: Finally, validation of the LPBF-printed component should be conducted to complete the closed-loop workflow. The distortion and residual stress levels of the fabricated component must be measured and compared with the predefined acceptance targets. If deviations occur, their root causes should be systematically diagnosed. This involves determining whether discrepancies originate from modeling assumptions in the prediction stage, process variability during manufacturing, powder or atmosphere drift, or insufficient post-treatment. Such source-based diagnosis prevents unnecessary adjustments within the wrong stage of the workflow. The results of this analysis can then guide updates to both the predictive models and the manufacturing process. For example, inherent strain parameters or thermal boundary conditions may be recalibrated using experimentally measured distortion and residual stress data. At the same time, the qualified process window should be documented, including process parameter boundaries, scan strategies, powder reuse limits, atmosphere control thresholds, and post-treatment schedules. Once validated, the outcome should be a transferable manufacturing route, consisting of a calibrated predictive model framework, a robust printing process recipe, a material and environmental control protocol, and a defined post-treatment specification, accompanied by inspection checkpoints for quality assurance. This integrated framework enables residual-stress-controlled LPBF manufacturing to transition from laboratory-scale optimization to reliable and repeatable industrial production (Fig.  22 ). sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook
paragraphs: Residual stress is an intrinsic consequence of the extreme thermal gradients, rapid solidification, and repeated thermal cycling inherent to LPBF, and it directly governs distortion, cracking susceptibility, dimensional consistency, and fatigue reliability of fabricated components. The mitigation of residual stress cannot be reliably achieved through a single control parameter. Instead, it must be addressed as a system-level challenge that encompasses simulation prediction, in-process manufacturing control, material design, and post-build engineering. Accordingly, this review consolidates the existing approaches into four interconnected strategies, including simulation-based prediction, manufacturing strategy optimization, material-level optimization, and post-treatment management. Furthermore, it highlights how these strategies can be integrated into a practical and actionable workflow, providing guidance for both fundamental research and industrial implementation of residual-stress-controlled LPBF manufacturing.

Multiscale simulation forms the backbone of a residual-stress control framework, as it provides quantitative insight into thermal history, constraint evolution, and stress accumulation, which are difficult to measure experimentally during the LPBF process. Accurate prediction of residual stress distribution depends on selecting an appropriate modeling fidelity that matches the targeted scale and decision requirements, ranging from high-fidelity thermo-mechanical models to computationally efficient approaches such as inherent-strain-based methods for predicting part-scale distortion and residual stress. When properly calibrated and experimentally validated, these models enable the identification of high-risk geometries, critical scan-path transitions, and stress concentration regions, thereby guiding support design and process parameter selection prior to printing. Thus, simulation becomes most valuable when it is used as a decision-support tool, rather than merely as a post hoc explanation of experimental observations, and when its predictions are continuously refined through experimental validation.

In-process residual stress mitigation represents a critical step following simulation-based prediction, as model outputs can be systematically leveraged to guide manufacturing optimization strategies. Such predictions enable the precise refinement of process parameters, scanning strategies, and structural design, thereby reducing residual stress while maintaining component quality. Optimization of process parameters, scan sequencing and patterns, preheating conditions, remelting strategies, and support or structural design can significantly reshape thermal gradients and constraint-induced shrinkage, helping to reduce stress accumulation while preserving part density and manufacturing productivity. Beyond these direct process controls, data-driven optimization and machine-learning-assisted parameter selection are increasingly valuable for accelerating multi-variable process exploration, particularly when residual stress must be balanced simultaneously with porosity control, microstructure evolution, and build rate.

Material-level optimization is equally important, as raw materials and environmental conditions must be carefully controlled to ensure consistency between simulation predictions and real manufacturing conditions. Key approaches include powder reuse governance to minimize variability, atmosphere control to stabilize chemical composition and defect formation, and transformation engineering to introduce beneficial strain accommodation during cooling for suitable alloy systems. Furthermore, grain refinement strategies and inoculant additions can improve plastic compatibility and reduce cracking susceptibility, thereby enhancing the ability of the material to accommodate residual stress. In situ alloying further expands the available design space for tailoring processability and stress accommodation. However, this approach requires strict control of compositional uniformity and microstructural stability, in order to avoid introducing new sources of residual stress or brittle phases during fabrication.

Post-treatment serves both as a route for residual stress elimination and as a means to tailor the final stress state for service performance. Global stress-relief heat treatment remains the most established approach for reducing residual stress through temperature-dependent yielding and time-dependent stress relaxation, and it is often required to achieve dimensional stability prior to machining or service. Mechanical and hybrid approaches, such as vibration stress relief and thermal vibration stress relief, provide lower-temperature alternatives for stress mitigation. However, their effectiveness and spatial uniformity depend strongly on component geometry, fixturing conditions, and the efficiency of vibration energy transmission. Surface-based treatments, including shot peening and laser shock peening, primarily introduce beneficial compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region, accompanied by microstructural refinement. These modifications can significantly improve fatigue resistance, wear performance, and resistance to environmental cracking. Such techniques are generally most effective when combined with global stress-relief processes and subsequent surface-finishing operations. Consequently, post-treatment strategies should be selected according to both residual-stress reduction targets and service performance requirements.

A practical residual-stress mitigation workflow for LPBF can be organized into four interconnected stages. First, accurate modeling of the LPBF process should be conducted according to the targeted scale and decision requirements. Simulation tools can then be used to predict thermal gradients, distortion tendencies, and high-stress regions for the target geometry, while also screening candidate scan strategies and support layouts before manufacturing. Second, manufacturing strategy optimization should be implemented based on simulation predictions. This stage involves selecting appropriate process parameters, scan patterns, layer sequencing strategies, and preheating or remelting schemes that minimize thermal gradients and constraint accumulation, while ensuring that density and productivity targets are maintained. Third, material-level optimization should be applied to ensure consistency with simulation assumptions and to stabilize the processable parameter window that governs stress sensitivity. This includes powder state management, atmosphere control, microstructure refinement, and alloy design strategies, such as transformation-assisted stress accommodation or in situ alloying, when appropriate. Fourth, post-treatment management should be implemented to achieve the final residual stress state and property profile required for service. This typically involves combining global stress-relief treatments with targeted surface stress engineering methods when enhanced fatigue or stress-corrosion resistance is required. Across all stages, the workflow should operate as a closed-loop system. Measurements of residual stress, distortion inspection, and mechanical performance validation should continuously feed back into model calibration and process strategy refinement, thereby improving process repeatability.

It should be noted that the proposed workflow serves as a general framework that incorporates most of the key factors and solutions relevant to residual stress reduction in LPBF processes. Nevertheless, it cannot encompass all occasional events or application-specific situations, and therefore should be adaptively modified according to the working conditions and performance requirements of different applications. For applications with low sensitivity to residual stress, these techniques should be selected purposefully. Furthermore, LPBF manufacturing is a comprehensive process that requires synergistic advances in simulation techniques, materials science, monitoring techniques, structural design, and characterization strategies. Consequently, future progress will rely on the deeper integration of modeling, sensing, and process control to establish a predictive and adaptive manufacturing pipeline for residual stress management. Several key research directions remain critical. First, standardized residual stress metrics are needed to link part-scale distortion risk with microstructure-scale stress states, enabling consistent comparison across materials, geometries, and manufacturing systems. Second, robust calibration protocols must be developed to ensure that simulation models and process optimization strategies can be reliably transferred across different machines, powder batches, and processing environments. Third, multi-objective optimization frameworks are required to simultaneously consider residual stress, porosity, microstructure evolution, surface integrity, and manufacturing throughput. In addition, future studies should place greater emphasis on workflow-level reliability, prioritizing repeatability and uncertainty quantification rather than focusing solely on peak stress reduction. This perspective is essential because industrial adoption depends not only on performance improvements but also on process consistency across builds and production environments. Finally, the integration of alloy design strategies for stress accommodation with real-time thermal management and targeted post-treatment approaches is likely to enable the next step change in residual stress controllability.
